may necessitate repeat imaging and treatment replanning. 

When radiation is given with definitive intent, the dosages prescribed for 
gross disease are fairly standard, usually in the range of 70 Gy (at 
approximately 2 Gy/fraction/day) for the following sites: lip, oral cavity, 
nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, glottic larynx, supraglottic larynx, 
occult primary, salivary gland tumors, and MM. A second dose (often 
approximately 60 Gy, but it can vary) may be used to cover peritumoral or 
nodal volumes at the highest risk for microscopic spread, while a lower 
dose (often approximately 50 Gy, but it can vary) is used for volumes 
treated electively or prophylactically with a low risk for microscopic spread. 

Although several palliative RT regimens are provided, no single regimen is 
always preferred152-155; specific prescriptions vary widely among NCCN 
Member Institutions. Any palliative RT regimen that might cause severe 
toxicities should be avoided. Hypofractionated regimens may be useful for 
patients with limited life expectancy, such as a few months. For example, 
a common version of the QUAD SHOT regimen consists of a dose of 44.4 
Gy, delivered in 12 fractions over three cycles, with each cycle separated 
by 2 to 3 weeks.156,157 In general, doses of 3-4 Gy/fractions are common in 
palliative schedules, although some institutions use larger fraction sizes 
delivered less frequently such as 6 to 8 Gy.158 

Radiation Doses 
Selection of an exact radiation dose prescription and schedule of delivery 
depends on the primary tumor and neck node size, whether altered 
fractionation is used, and clinical circumstances, including whether 
concurrent systemic therapy will be used (see Principles of Radiation 
Techniques and the individual Principles of Radiation Therapy for each 
primary site in the algorithm). The dose may need to be decreased if it is 
prescribed very close to the adjacent organ(s) at risk (eg, brain, cochlea, 
optic chiasm and nerves, spinal cord). In these cases, precise target 
definition and delineation is crucial, and on-treatment imaging should be 
used to ensure accurate radiation delivery. Anatomical changes (eg, 

When treating definitively using conventional fractionation, the primary 
tumor and involved lymph nodes (ie, high-risk sites) generally require a 
total of 66 Gy (2.0–2.2 Gy/fraction) to 70 Gy (2.0 Gy/fraction).159-162 For 
areas considered highly sensitive to radiation, such as neural structures, 
some clinicians advocate that the fractionation should be slightly modified 
(eg, <2.0 Gy/fraction for at least some of the treatment) to minimize 
toxicity. In these cases, additional fractions can be added depending on 
clinical circumstances to increase the total physical dose. For instance, a 
hyperfractionated schedule allows gross disease to be prescribed a dose 
of up to 81.6 Gy (at 1.2 Gy/fraction); hyperfractionation has been used for 
situations when tumor is abutting brain or optic structures.159,160 Care must 
be taken if prescribed doses exceed 72 Gy using conventional 
fractionation (2.0 Gy/fraction), as this may lead to unacceptable rates of 
normal tissue injury; however, these data were collected in the era prior to 
advanced techniques such as IMRT or IMPT.159,163 In contrast, when using 
conventional fractionation, elective irradiation to low- and intermediate-risk 
sites is usually prescribed at 44 Gy (2.0 Gy/fraction) to 63 Gy (1.6–1.8 
Gy/fraction), depending on the estimated risk of tumor involvement, and 
on whether three-dimensional (3D) conformal RT (3D-CRT) or IMRT is 
used. For 3D-CRT and sequential plans using IMRT, a range of 44–50 Gy 
(2.0 Gy/fraction) is often suggested.164,165 For simultaneous integrated 
boost (SIB) IMRT, a range of doses from 54–63 Gy (1.6–1.8 Gy/fraction) is 
often used depending on the overall time of the radiation course and the 
risk of tumor involvement in the area where the dose is prescribed.165-167 In 
definitive RT, the delivery of six fractions per week is widely accepted, in a 
mildly accelerated schedule, especially if chemotherapy is not prescribed 
concurrently.161 Hypofractionation, when RT is given at >3.0 Gy/fraction, 
has been reported in some single institutional experiences and clinical 
trials,154,156,168,169 but a lack of high-level randomized comparator data and

recurrence rates with daily fraction sizes <200 cGy where the cumulative 
weekly dose is <1000 cGy.178,179 

Postoperative irradiation is recommended based on stage, histology, and 
surgical-pathologic findings. In general, postoperative RT is recommended 
for selected risk factors, including advanced T stage, close surgical 
margins, depth or extent of invasion, multiple positive nodes, or 
perineural/lymphovascular invasion. High doses of postoperative RT alone 
(eg, 66 Gy) and/or systemic therapy/RT are recommended for the 
high-risk features of ENE and/or positive margins.141,142,162 For these high-
risk cases in particular, the preferred maximum elapsed time interval 
between surgical resection and the start of postoperative RT is ≤6 
weeks.170 

Postoperative radiation fractionation schedules tend to be similar (60–66 
Gy at 2 Gy/fraction) whether or not systemic therapy is administered 
concurrently with postoperative RT. One exception is for postoperative 
irradiation of surgically resected HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer, 
where some institutions deliver a lower dosage to part or all of the 
postoperative volume.171 Hypofractionation may be considered for patients 
who are not good candidates for an extended course of several weeks of 
RT due to resource limitations or comorbidities; however, these schedules 
continue to be tested in early-phase trials, as late effects are a particular 
concern in the postoperative population.172 

Two large randomized trials from Europe have reported improved 
locoregional control using altered fractionation as compared to 
conventional fractionation, when concurrent chemotherapy is not given. 
The EORTC protocol 22791 compared hyperfractionation (1.15 Gy twice 
daily, or 80.5 Gy over 7 weeks) with conventional fractionation (2 Gy once 
daily, or 70 Gy over 7 weeks) in the treatment of T2, T3, N0–1 
oropharyngeal carcinoma excluding base of tongue primaries. At 5 years, 
a statistically significant increase in local control was observed in the 
hyperfractionation arm (38% vs. 56%; P = .01) and no increase in late 
complications was observed.180 A long-term follow-up analysis has also 
shown a small survival advantage for hyperfractionation (P = .05).181 
Another EORTC protocol (22851) compared accelerated fractionation (1.6 
Gy 3 times daily, or 72 Gy over 5 weeks) with conventional fractionation 
(1.8–2.0 Gy once daily, or 70 Gy over 7–8 weeks) in various intermediate 
to advanced H&N cancers (excluding cancers of the hypopharynx). 
Patients in the accelerated fractionation arm had significantly better 
locoregional control at 5 years (P = .02). Disease-specific survival (DSS) 
showed a trend in favor of the accelerated fractionation arm (P = .06). 
However, acute and late toxicity were increased with acceleration, raising 
questions about the net advantages of accelerated fractionation.182 

The RTOG reported the results of a four-arm, phase III, randomized 
clinical trial (RTOG 90-03) comparing hyperfractionation and two variants 
of accelerated fractionation versus standard fractionation.159,160,183 After 2 
years of follow-up, both accelerated fractionation arms using either a 
concomitant boost (AFX-C) or hyperfractionation were associated with 
improved locoregional control and DFS, as compared with standard 
fractionation. Acute toxicity was increased with both of these regimens. 

Fractionation in RT Alone 
No single fractionation schedule has proven to be best for all tumors. Data 
strongly indicate that SCCHN can grow rapidly and may compensate for 
RT-induced cell loss through the mechanism of accelerated 
repopulation.173,174 Especially in the RT-alone setting, schedules delivering 
at least 1000 cGy per week to gross disease are recommended,175-177 
although it is acknowledged that some tumors such as those of the 
salivary gland may have slower cell kinetics. Trials and institutional

multiagent systemic therapy, and altered fractionation schedules with 
concurrent systemic therapy have been evaluated alone or in combination. 
Numerous trials have shown that altered fractionation and concurrent 
chemotherapy are more efficacious than altered fractionation alone.188-190 
However, conversely, the GORTEC 99-02 trial reported that altered 
fractionation did not improve outcomes when compared with conventional 
fractionation given with concurrent chemotherapy.191,192 Likewise, RTOG 
0129 assessed accelerated fractionation with two cycles of concurrent 
cisplatin versus standard fractionation with three cycles of concurrent 
cisplatin. There was no significant difference in OS between the two 
arms,27,193,194 indicating that accelerated fractionation is not clearly more 
efficacious than conventional fractionation in the setting of concurrent 
chemotherapy. 

The MARCH meta-analysis, including individual patient data from 15 
randomized trials, analyzed the effect of hyperfractionated or accelerated 
RT on survival of patients with H&N cancers.184 Standard fractionation 
constituted the control arm in all of the trials in this meta-analysis.161 An 
absolute survival benefit for altered fractionation of 3.4% at 5 years (HR, 
0.92; 95% CI, 0.86–0.97; P = .003) was reported. This benefit, however, 
was limited to patients <60 years of age.184 Hyperfractionation was 
associated with a benefit of 8% after 5 years.185 An update to the MARCH 
meta-analysis, including data from 33 trials, continued to show a survival 
benefit of hyperfractionation, compared to standard fractionation (HR, 
0.83; 95% CI, 0.74–0.92; P < .001), in patients with locally advanced 
SCCHN.186 

Consensus on the optimal use of altered fractionation schedules using 
either concomitant boost or hyperfractionation for stage III or IV oral cavity, 
oropharynx, supraglottic larynx, and hypopharyngeal squamous cell 
cancers has not yet emerged among NCCN Member Institutions.184,187,188 
The logistical difficulties of twice-daily radiation treatments are a 
consideration on the individual patient level. Furthermore, as described 
below, using altered fractionation in conjunction with most concurrent 
systemic agents remains controversial. 

Concurrent chemoradiation increases acute toxicity compared to radiation 
alone, although an increase in late toxicity beyond that caused by RT 
alone has been less clearly established in prospective clinical trials.195-197 
However, individual chemotherapy agents, especially cisplatin, are well 
known to introduce late toxicities including fatigue, cognitive impairment, 
hearing loss, peripheral neuropathy, infertility, early menopause, 
osteoporosis, and an increased risk of secondary cancers or 
cardiovascular issues.198 Multiagent systemic therapy may further increase 
the acute and late toxicity burden.199 Immunotherapy is increasingly being 
used in multimodality paradigms involving RT and is associated with a 
number of well-characterized toxicities. In planning any systemic therapy, 
close attention should be paid to published reports for the specific 
systemic agent, dose, and schedule of administration. In particular, 
systemic therapy delivery concurrent with radiation should be performed

radiation in combination with most concurrent systemic therapies in the 
definitive treatment setting. Most published studies have used 
conventional fractionation (at 2.0 Gy/fraction to a typical dose of 70 Gy in 7

Radiation Techniques 

IMRT 
Using contemporary computer-based planning and radiation delivery, the 
intensity of the radiation beam can be modulated to decrease doses to 
normal structures with minimal compromise of the doses to the cancer 
targets.200,201 Over the last 15 years, IMRT has displaced older techniques 
in the treatment of most H&N malignancies and when available, is 
currently preferred by the Panel for most clinical situations.202-209 IMRT is a 
highly advanced form of CRT permitting more precise cancer targeting 
while reducing dose to normal tissues.165,210-213 

IMRT is now the predominant technique used at NCCN Member 
Institutions.220,221 OS may be similar between patients treated with IMRT 
and those receiving conventional 3D-RT,202,222-224 but both are superior to 
older two-dimensional (2D) techniques. For example, a prospective 
Korean study showed that 3D and IMRT techniques were superior to 2D 
radiation for both PFS and OS in patients with NPC, and IMRT was 
associated with improved survival in multivariate analysis, particularly in 
T3–T4 tumors.225 In addition, IMRT has been clearly proven to reduce 
long-term toxicities. Numerous phase II and III studies show that IMRT 
decreases late toxicity (xerostomia) without compromising tumor control 
for nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, sinonasal, and other sites. 

Xerostomia is a common long-term side effect of RT, which is ameliorated 
most commonly by use of IMRT, or from application of drug therapy (eg, 
pilocarpine, cevimeline), salivary substitutes, and other novel approaches 
(eg, surgical relocation of submandibular gland).207,226-230 Importantly, rates 
of severe xerostomia have decreased due to the transition from older 2D 
and 3D radiotherapy techniques to IMRT.202,204 Pow et al evaluated 
treatment of early-stage NPC with conventional RT techniques versus with 
IMRT.227 The results showed a statistical improvement in salivary flow and 
in patient-reported QOL parameters.227 Kam et al’s study assigned 
patients with NPC to either IMRT or conventional 2D-RT.207 At 1 year after 
treatment, patients in the IMRT arm had significantly lower rates of 
clinician-rated severe xerostomia than patients in the 2D-RT arm (39.3% 
vs. 82.1%; P = .001). Salivary flow rates were also higher with IMRT. The 
mean parotid dose was 32 Gy in the IMRT group and 62 Gy in the 
conventional group. Although a trend for improvement in patient-reported 
dry mouth was observed after IMRT, recovery was incomplete and there 
was no significant difference in patient-reported outcomes between the 

IMRT dose painting, also known as SIB, refers to the method of assigning 
different dose levels to different anatomical areas. These areas are all 
simultaneously irradiated within the same treatment fraction but receive 
different prescribed doses (eg, 2.0 Gy/fraction to gross tumor, 1.6 
Gy/fraction to neck at risk for microscopic tumor, <1.0 Gy/fraction to 
parotid gland) resulting in different total doses to the different targets and 
organs (eg, 70 Gy, 56 Gy, <26 Gy).214,215 Although dose painting has been 
used to improve the specificity of radiation delivery to tumors and thereby 
reduce unwanted radiation of uninvolved areas, hot spots associated with 
higher toxicity can occur within large tumor targets due to the increasing 
heterogeneity of dose distribution that occurs when prescribing to large 
volumes.215,216 An alternative to the dose painting or SIB approach is to 
create two plans, one irradiating widely to a low dose and a separate 
boost plan boosting specific areas to a higher dose. The boost plan may 
be delivered after completion of the initial plan, or the two plans may be 
delivered on the same day as separate fractions in twice-daily schemas 
(see Principles of Radiation Techniques in the algorithm).161,212,217,218 A 
meta-analysis including seven studies (n = 1049) showed no significant

There are numerous other specific advantages of IMRT that apply to 
challenging anatomical situations. IMRT is particularly useful in avoiding 
excess radiation of the optic pathway in patients with sinonasal 
malignancies.232 However, the randomized phase III COSTAR trial did not 
show that cochlear-sparing IMRT significantly reduced hearing loss in 
patients with parotid tumors, compared to 3D-CRT.237 One caveat is that 
additional care must be taken when using IMRT as it can create 
unanticipated toxicities to organs unexpectedly radiated in the beam path. 
A careful and dosimetrically informed examination of all organs potentially 
affected by these novel distributions of the radiation dose is 
mandatory.240,241

were included. Grade 2 or worse (LENT-SOMA scale) xerostomia 2 years

versus 29% of patients in the IMRT group (P < .0001). No differences 
were seen in the rates of locoregional control or survival. Most recently, a 
fourth trial, GORTEC 2004-01, showed that dose-escalated IMRT (50 Gy 
in 25 fractions followed by a sequential boost of 25 Gy in 10 fractions), 
delivered concurrently with cisplatin, reduced xerostomia in patients with 
locally advanced SCCHN, as compared to the control arm of 3D-RT (50 
Gy in 25 fractions followed by a sequential boost of 20 Gy in 10 fractions) 
delivered concurrently with cisplatin (23% vs. 63%, respectively, after 1 
year, and 11% vs. 45%, respectively, after 3 years).231 Locoregional 
control did not significantly differ between the two study arms. 

Proton Beam Therapy 
At present, proton therapy is the predominant particle therapy under active 
clinical investigation in the United States.242-245 Proton therapy has been 
used in the treatment of skull base tumors, oropharyngeal cancers, 
sinonasal malignancies, adenoid cystic carcinomas, and MMs.246-254 
Proton therapy has typically been used to treat patients with the most 
challenging disease configurations, for which other RT options were not 
felt to be safe or of any benefit.249,255,256 Proton therapy has also been 
proposed for children and young adults where a reduced exposure to low-
level falloff radiation dose is an appealing feature. 

Until recently, data supporting the use of proton beam therapy (PBT) has 
come mainly from nonrandomized institutional reports and a small number 
of systematic reviews. A systematic review and meta-analysis of non-
comparative observation studies concluded that patients with malignant 
diseases of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses who received proton 
therapy appeared to have better outcomes than those receiving photon 
therapy.257 A review of proton therapy in patients with H&N cancers 
included 14 retrospective reviews and four prospective nonrandomized 

IMRT likely reduces other long-term toxicities due to decreased radiation 
doses to structures such as pharyngeal constrictors, larynx, temporal 
lobes, mandible, auditory structures (including cochlea), and optic 
structures.166,207,227,232-237 For instance, in the randomized phase III DARS 
trial from the UK and Ireland, a dysphagia-optimized IMRT intervention in 
which the constrictor muscles of the pharynx were spared improved 
swallowing outcomes at 12 months compared to standard IMRT (P = .037) 
in patients with early-stage and locally advanced cancers of the 
oropharynx or hypopharynx.238 Other retrospective analyses, including one 
of 2993 patients who received RT for treatment of H&N cancer, have 
shown that patients who received IMRT had a shorter duration of feeding

In institutional series, the reported outcomes for proton therapy have 
included good locoregional control, freedom from distant metastasis, and 
acceptable toxicity.243,251,254,258-261 PBT may be associated with even 
greater normal tissue sparing without sacrificing target coverage, which is 
hypothesized to be associated with reduced toxicity compared to IMRT.258 
This may be a particular advantage in cases of reirradiation.262

recent clinical trials in locoregionally advanced oropharyngeal cancer have 
confirmed that outcomes with intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) 
are very comparable to those obtained with IMRT. A multicenter 
randomized phase III trial assigned 440 patients to definitive treatment 
based on either IMRT or IMPT and showed that 3-year PFS rates were 
83.0% and 82.5%, respectively, thus fulfilling the primary endpoint of non-
inferiority. PFS rates at 5 years were 76.2% and 81.3%, respectively, and

United Kingdom, TORPEDO, included 205 similarly randomized patients 
and reported 2-year freedom from locoregional recurrence rates of 94% 
for IMPT versus 97% for IMRT. At this shorter follow-up, there was no 
difference seen in OS rates, which were 95% versus 95%, respectively. 
Co-primary endpoints of this trial were 12-month gastrostomy tube 
dependence or weight loss ≥20% from baseline as well as the UW-QOL 
mean physical composite score. None of these were significantly 
different.271 

However, the planning and delivery of PBT continues to develop, and 
occasional fatal outcomes have been reported with proton therapy due to 
uncertainties associated with these evolving technologies, including a 
small number of deaths secondary to brainstem injury in children.263-265 In 
general, clinicians have reported low rates of serious toxicities when using 
strict dose limits for proton therapy.255,266 However, disadvantageous and 
advantageous outcomes continue to be more fully documented as the 
clinical experience accrues. A pooled analysis of 17 studies including 
patients with H&N cancer treated with PBT showed a rate of grade ≥3 
osteoradionecrosis of 0.01 (95% CI, 0.01–0.03),267 although retrospective 
analyses have shown increased potential for this complication in single-
institutional experiences.268 In patients who have tumors that are 
periocular in location and/or invade the orbit, skull base, and/or cavernous 
sinus, or whose primary tumors extend intracranially or exhibit extensive 
perineural invasion, highly conformal dose distributions are crucial, and 
proton therapy may provide certain unique advantages. In patients with 
these types of tumors who are being treated with curative intent and/or 
have long life expectancies, PBT may offer the opportunity for lower late-
onset toxicities.269 

From these randomized trial data, it is thus proven that IMPT is an 
effective and safe treatment that produces non-inferior oncologic 
outcomes for oropharyngeal cancers. However, it is premature to conclude 
that proton therapy has been established as invariably superior to other 
modern radiation techniques such as IMRT, particularly with regard to 
tumor control. Nonetheless, given the unique abilities of PBT to treat more 
difficult tumors, randomized trials may not be possible for some clinical 
scenarios. In these cases, an alternative approach developing 
prospectively maintained databases to raise the quality of institutional 
reports of clinical experiences is strongly encouraged.265 In other H&N 
cancers specifically including those of the supraglottic larynx, 
nasopharynx, paranasal sinus, and salivary glands, as well as MM, and 
unknown primary tumors of the H&N, the Panel agrees that proton therapy

Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy 
Stereotactic body RT (SBRT) is an advanced technique of external beam 
RT (EBRT) that delivers large ablative doses of radiation in a limited 
number of fractions. Advantages of SBRT include a shorter overall 
treatment time, promising local control, and higher but acceptable toxicity 
depending on the specific location treated.274 There is currently insufficient 
evidence to recommend SBRT routinely for treatment of H&N cancers, but 
the NCCN Panel acknowledges that it might be beneficial in the settings of 
re-irradiation, palliation, or for older adults.275-277 

Brachytherapy 
Brachytherapy is a uniquely conformal modality that is effective and safe 
when delivered by an experienced team of practitioners. Brachytherapy is 
now necessary less often because of improved local control and lower 
toxicities obtained with IMRT with or without systemic therapy. However, 
brachytherapy still has an important role in cancers of the lip and oral 
cavity (see Cancer of the Oral Cavity [Including Mucosal Lip]: Principles of 
Radiation Therapy in the algorithm).272 Brachytherapy may have a role in 
other select clinical scenarios such as reirradiation, as a boost for highly 
refractory disease or a positive surgical margin, or when extremely 
conformal radiation delivery is needed to a very well-defined tumor 
location. These are unique situations arising from challenging clinical 
circumstances and limited availability of H&N brachytherapy expertise. 

One emerging setting where SBRT has been of increasing interest is 
oligometastatic disease. In the GORTEC OMET phase II trial, in which 69 
patients having oligometastatic H&N cancers were randomized to receive 
SBRT with or without EXTREME-based chemotherapy, the median 
survival was 42.3 months (95% CI, 26.5–not reached) with chemotherapy-
SBRT and 41.1 months (95% CI, 32.1–66.9) with SBRT alone.278 A 
systematic review and meta-analysis including eight retrospective studies 
(N = 352) of patients with oligometastatic SCCHN found that SBRT was 
the most used radical treatment.279 Local control rates ranged from 75% to 
97.8% at year 1 and from 57% to 94.4% at 2 years. Treatment-related 
toxicity was low across all studies, with grade ≥3 toxicity being rare, 
especially when SBRT was used alone. 

The potential for brachytherapy to reduce side effects, because of its 
uniquely conformal radiation dose distribution, remains a matter of debate. 
A randomized trial investigated the reduction in xerostomia at 6 months, 
assessed using 99mTc salivary scintigraphy, in patients receiving IMRT or 
IMRT combined with brachytherapy in patients with T1–T2, N0, M0 
oropharyngeal SCC.273 Ninety patients were randomized, but evaluation 
was not possible in 20 patients at 6 months. In the remaining 70 
participants, scintigraphy-determined xerostomia rates were 14% and 44% 
in the brachytherapy-containing and IMRT-alone arms, respectively. 

Recently, prospective data have been reported using highly conformal 
stereotactic RT in the management of early-stage glottic larynx cancer. In 
the GLoTtic Larynx-SABR phase II trial, 25 patients with stage 0–II SCC of 
the glottic larynx received stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) 
delivered in 5 fractions (N = 21) or 16 fractions (N = 4).280 At a median 
follow-up of 3.7 years, there were 2 in-field recurrences (1 per dose 
cohort). The cumulative local failure rate was 4% (90% CI, 0.8%–20%)

Treatment that includes systemic therapy of H&N cancers is 
recommended for locoregionally advanced and recurrent or metastatic 
disease. This section describes systemic therapy for locally advanced 
SCCHN with perioperative or adjuvant immunotherapy and concurrent or 
sequential RT-based treatment. 

SBRT has been reported in numerous retrospective reviews in the 
reirradiation setting.282 Careful anticipation of toxicity is especially 
important in planning the delivery of this modality to a patient. Small 
prospective studies have aimed at the purpose of demonstrating safety 
and feasibility in combination with systemic therapies including cetuximab 
or cisplatin, but continued documentation of clinical outcomes is advised 
due to the relatively limited experience with combining these 
modalities.283,284 

In patients with resectable locally advanced and newly diagnosed 
recurrent or metastatic SCCHN, testing for programmed death ligand 1 
(PD-L1) combined positive score (CPS) should be performed to guide 
treatment decisions. In patients with recurrent or metastatic SCCHN, 
multigene panel testing for biomarker identification of actionable genomic 
alterations and quantification of tumor mutational burden (TMB) and 
selective immunohistochemistry (IHC) testing (HER2 and mismatch repair 
[MMR]/microsatellite instability [MSI] status) for actionable protein 
expression patterns may be considered to guide treatment options. 

For detailed recommendations on combination and single-agent systemic 
therapy for metastatic (M1) disease at presentation (without surgery or RT 
treatment), see the section below under Very Advanced Head and Neck 
Cancers. Systemic therapy/RT for locoregionally advanced 
nasopharyngeal cancer is described below under Cancer of the 
Nasopharynx. 

Follow-up After RT 
For patients whose cancer has been treated with RT, the recommended 
follow-up (see Follow-up Recommendations in the algorithm) includes an 
assessment of thyroid function (ie, the thyroid-stimulating hormone [TSH] 
level should be determined every 6–12 months) and surveillance-oriented 
physical examination, symptom assessment and supportive care, and/or 
imaging as clinically indicated. Increased TSH levels have been detected 
in 20% to 25% of patients who have received neck irradiation.285-287 
Changes in TSH may indicate thyroid gland dysfunction or hypopituitarism 
if the skull base was irradiated. For patients with signs or symptoms or 
who are at high risk for hypopituitarism, screening laboratories may 
include growth hormone (GH), follicle-stimulating hormone/luteinizing 
hormone (FSH/LH), free T4, insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), TSH, 
adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), and prolactin. 

Systemic Therapy with Concurrent RT 
Randomized trials144,288-296 and meta-analyses297-301 showed significantly 
improved OS, DFS, and locoregional control when a systemic therapy and 
RT regimen (concomitant or, less commonly, sequential) was compared 
with RT alone for locally advanced disease. Limited data are available 
comparing the efficacy of different chemoradiotherapy regimens.

was more common with the weekly cisplatin regimen. 

Based on all available data, high-dose cisplatin with RT is the preferred 
systemic therapy/RT regimen for cisplatin-eligible patients with unresected 
or resected locally advanced SCCHN. However, if the clinician has a 
patient-specific concern about the toxicity of high-dose cisplatin, a weekly 
cisplatin regimen at a dose of 40 mg/m2/week may be substituted. Weekly 
doses of cisplatin of <40 mg/m2 should not be utilized in this setting 
because survival outcomes were inferior. In the absence of confirmatory 
and mature prospective comparison trials, it is unclear whether low-dose 
weekly cisplatin is either less toxic or equally efficacious as high-dose 
cisplatin in this setting. The categories of evidence for other systemic 
(non–cisplatin-containing chemotherapy) regimens that are perceived to 
be better tolerated are much lower than for high-dose cisplatin. A 
randomized phase III trial showed that DFS and OS were better with 
docetaxel and RT compared to RT alone among cisplatin-ineligible 
patients with locally advanced SCCHN.145 However, moderate to severe 
mucositis, odynophagia, and dysphagia were more common with the 
addition of docetaxel to RT, which may limit the application of this regimen 
to patients who are frail. The role of other systemic therapy regimens with 
RT is unclear in patients with locally advanced SCCHN. 

Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) overexpression is common in 
SCCHN and is associated with poor survival outcomes.306,307 Bonner et al 
randomly assigned 424 patients with locally advanced stage III–IV SCC of 
the hypopharynx, oropharynx, and larynx to receive definitive RT with or 
without cetuximab.308 Locoregional control and median OS (49 vs. 29.3 
months; P = .03) were significantly improved in patients treated with RT 
and cetuximab compared to RT alone. Five-year OS was 45.6% in 
patients treated with RT and cetuximab and 36.4% in patients who 
received RT alone (HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.56–0.95; P = .018).309 Infusion 

High-dose cisplatin plus RT is the most studied effective systemic 
therapy/RT regimen and typically uses conventional fractionation or RT at 
2.0 Gy per fraction to 70 Gy administered over 7 weeks with concurrent 
high-dose cisplatin 100 mg/m2 given every 3 weeks for up to three 
doses.162,288 Because of perceived lower toxicity, low-dose once-a-week 
cisplatin has been studied. A randomized phase III trial compared cisplatin 
20 mg/m2 given once weekly with RT to definitive RT alone to patients with 
locally advanced SCCHN and showed no improvement in survival 
outcomes with the weekly 20 mg/m2 cisplatin + RT regimen.302 A 
randomized phase III trial compared cisplatin 30 mg/m2 given once weekly 
to high-dose cisplatin, both given with RT (93% of cases treated 
postoperatively) to patients with locally advanced SCCHN.143 The primary 
endpoint was locoregional control. Most patients (93%) received study 
treatment in the adjuvant setting. Locoregional control was inferior in the 
cisplatin 30 mg/m2 weekly arm compared to the high-dose cisplatin arm. 
The 2-year locoregional control rate was 58.5% in the low-dose weekly 
cisplatin arm and 73.1% in the high-dose cisplatin arm (P = .014). Acute 
toxicities of grade 3 or greater were less common in the low-dose weekly 
arm compared to the high-dose cisplatin arm (71.6% vs. 84.6%; P = .006). 
Long-term results from this trial confirmed the original findings that high-
dose cisplatin leads to superior locoregional control compared to cisplatin 
30 mg/m2 weekly.303 The updated 2-year and 5-year locoregional control 
rates were 58.75% and 48.09% in the low-dose weekly cisplatin arm and 
73.95% and 57.76% in the high-dose cisplatin arm, respectively (P = 
.034). A systematic review and meta-analysis including six randomized 
studies with 554 patients with SCCHN showed that OS, PFS, and toxicity 
did not significantly differ between weekly cisplatin and high-dose cisplatin 
(both given with RT).304 However, the subsequent JCOG1008 randomized 
phase II/III trial showed that chemoradiotherapy with weekly cisplatin at 40 
mg/m2 was non-inferior to high-dose every-3-week cisplatin with respect to 
OS in patients with high-risk, resected locally, advanced SCCHN.305 High-
grade neutropenia, infections, and renal and hearing impairment were less

hospitalization for toxicity (42% vs. 22%, respectively; P < .001) were 
more prevalent in patients who received cetuximab combined with 
carboplatin/fluorouracil and RT. Collectively, these data show that 
cetuximab combined with chemoradiation is not recommended.

10%), pruritus (16% vs. 4%), and headache (19% vs. 8%) were more

discontinued in 5.8% of patients due to infusion reactions or acneiform 
rash. Notably, to be eligible for this trial, patients were required to have 
normal renal, hepatic, and hematopoietic function and adequate PS. The 
role of RT and cetuximab compared to RT alone in patients who are frail 
and do not meet these eligibility criteria or in those who are not candidates 
for cisplatin has not been formally assessed in randomized phase III trials. 

The open-label, parallel-group, randomized phase II/III NRG-HN004 trial 
was designed to evaluate whether definitive RT combined with 
durvalumab, a PD-L1 inhibitor, would improve outcomes compared to RT 
and cetuximab.314 At 2 years, PFS was 50.6% (95% CI, 41.5–59.8) in the 
durvalumab arm versus 63.7% (95% CI, 51.3–76.1) in the cetuximab arm 
(HR 1.33; 95% CI, 0.84–2.12; P = .89). Adverse events were similar 
between both groups. The phase 3 part of the study was not conducted 
due to not meeting prespecified endpoints in the phase 2 analysis. 

In three randomized phase III trials, cetuximab and definitive RT was 
compared to cisplatin and definitive RT as a deintensification treatment 
strategy for HPV-positive locally advanced oropharyngeal cancer. These 
trials showed that cetuximab and RT was inferior to cisplatin and RT (in 
terms of OS) and was not better tolerated.315-317 In the RTOG 1016 trial, 
849 patients with locally advanced HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer 
were randomized to receive accelerated IMRT with either cetuximab or 
cisplatin.315 After a median follow-up of 4.5 years, the cetuximab arm did 
not meet the criterion for noninferiority (based on 5-year OS). Five-year 
OS was 77.9% for the cetuximab arm and 84.6% for the cisplatin arm. 
PFS and risk of locoregional failure were significantly worse in the 
cetuximab arm compared to the cisplatin arm (HR, 1.72; 95% CI, 1.29–
2.29; P < .001 for PFS; HR, 2.05; 95% CI, 1.35–3.10; P < .001 for 
locoregional failure). Five-year PFS and locoregional failure rates were 
67.3% and 17.3% for the cetuximab arm and 78.4% and 9.9% for the 
cisplatin arm, respectively. In the randomized phase III De-ESCALaTE 

The randomized phase III RTOG 0522 trial showed that the addition of 
cetuximab to cisplatin and definitive RT did not significantly improve OS, 
compared to cisplatin and RT, in patients with stage III or IV SCCHN 
and, importantly, was more toxic.310 Cetuximab added to RT resulted in 
more frequent interruptions in RT and grade 3 to 4 radiation mucositis, 
rash, fatigue, anorexia, and hypokalemia. Long-term updates from this 
trial confirmed the original findings of no improvement in outcomes with 
the addition of cetuximab to cisplatin and RT.311 At a median follow-up of 
10.1 years, the addition of cetuximab did not reduce the incidence of 
locoregional failure or distant metastasis, or improve OS. No 
improvement in PFS was reported in those with oropharyngeal cancer, 
regardless of p16 status, in the cetuximab arm. Consistent with the 
original data, rates of toxicity were higher in the cetuximab arm 
compared to the RT + cisplatin arm, at 61.3% and 57.4%, respectively. 
Similarly, a randomized phase II trial showed that the addition of the oral 
EGFR inhibitor erlotinib to definitive RT + cisplatin did not improve 
efficacy outcomes.312 In the phase III GORTEC 2007-01 trial, cetuximab 
combined with carboplatin/fluorouracil and RT was compared to 
cetuximab and RT.313 Three-year PFS (52.3% vs. 40.5%, respectively; 
HR, 0.73; 95% CI, 0.57–0.94; P = .015) and locoregional failure (21.6% 
vs. 38.8%, respectively; HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.38–0.76; P < .001) rates 
were better with the cetuximab and carboplatin/fluorouracil regimen, but

chemotherapy—used as part of a larynx preservation strategy—is listed as 
a category 2A designation. 

Panel members think that induction chemotherapy should only be 
administered at sites with expertise in these regimens because of 
challenges associated with appropriate patient selection and management 
of treatment-related toxicities.319 Residual toxicity from induction 
chemotherapy may complicate the subsequent delivery of definitive RT or 
systemic therapy/RT.

patients with locally advanced p16-positive oropharyngeal SCC.316 
Patients given cisplatin and RT had significantly better 2-year OS (97.5% 
vs. 89.4%, respectively; HR, 5.0; 95% CI, 1.7–14.7; P = .001) and a lower 
recurrence rate (6.0% vs. 16.1%, respectively; HR, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.6–7.2; 
P < .001) compared to patients given cetuximab and RT. In the multicenter 
TROG 12.01 trial, 189 patients with intermediate-risk HPV-positive 
oropharyngeal cancer were randomized to receive 70 Gy RT with either 
low-dose weekly cisplatin (40 mg/m2/week) or cetuximab.317 The 3-year 
failure-free survival was 93% in the RT/cisplatin arm and 80% in the 
RT/cetuximab arm (P = .015). These three phase III trials demonstrated 
that cetuximab and RT was inferior to cisplatin and RT in patients with 
HPV-positive locally advanced oropharyngeal cancer.315-317 

When concurrent systemic therapy/RT is recommended for treatment of 
locoregionally advanced HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, the Panel 
asserts that high-dose cisplatin is the preferred systemic agent, although 
low-dose (40 mg/m2) weekly cisplatin is also an option. An NRG trial is 
currently in progress for comparing high-dose cisplatin to low-dose weekly 
cisplatin in locally advanced SCCHN (Clinical trial ID: NCT05050162). 

A summary of the data helps provide perspective on the NCCN Panel’s 
recommendations. Most randomized trials comparing induction 
chemotherapy followed by RT and/or surgery to locoregional treatment 
alone did not show an improvement in OS with the incorporation of 
induction chemotherapy.299 However, in some studies, a lower rate of 
distant metastases was noted with induction chemotherapy.320 Also, a 
correlation was noted between favorable tumor response to induction 
chemotherapy and durable disease control with subsequent RT.320,321 
Thus, the hypothesis was developed that induction chemotherapy could 
facilitate organ preservation (by avoidance of total laryngectomy) and 
improve QOL of patients although OS was not improved. Because total 
laryngectomy is among the procedures most feared by patients,322 larynx 
preservation was the focus of initial studies of induction chemotherapy. 

Induction Chemotherapy 
The role of induction chemotherapy in the management of locally 
advanced SCCHN has generated considerable discussion and debate 
within the NCCN Panel. The lack of consensus among NCCN Member 
Institutions despite the extensive discussion is illustrated by the category 3 
recommendation (ie, major disagreement) for induction chemotherapy for 
the management of locoregionally advanced p16-negative and p16-
positive oropharyngeal cancer. However, in other sites of disease (glottic 
and supraglottic larynx and hypopharynx), induction chemotherapy is 
recommended based on an update from the RTOG 91-11 trial.318 For 
selected patients with hypopharyngeal and laryngeal cancers (with less 

Two randomized studies—the Veterans Affairs (VA) Laryngeal Cancer 
Study Group trial in advanced larynx cancer and the EORTC trial in 
advanced hypopharynx cancer—established the role of induction 
cisplatin/fluorouracil followed by definitive RT in patients with disease 
responsive to induction chemotherapy as an alternative treatment to total 
laryngectomy and postoperative RT, offering potential larynx preservation 
without compromising OS (see Cancer of the Larynx and Cancer of the 
Hypopharynx in this Discussion).320,321 Although locally relapsed/refractory

phase III trials compared induction cisplatin plus fluorouracil with or 
without the addition of a taxane (docetaxel or paclitaxel) followed by the 
same locoregional treatment in both groups. Results showed significantly 
improved outcomes (response rates, DFS, or OS, depending on the trial) 
for patients in the three-drug induction group (taxane plus cisplatin and 
fluorouracil) compared to those receiving two drugs (cisplatin plus 
fluorouracil).328-331 A randomized phase III trial in the larynx preservation 
setting similarly showed superior larynx preservation outcome with 
induction TPF (docetaxel, cisplatin, and fluorouracil) compared to 
cisplatin/fluorouracil.332,333 A meta-analysis including five randomized 
controlled trials (RCTs) (N = 1772) showed that the TPF induction 
chemotherapy regimen, compared to cisplatin plus fluorouracil, was 
associated with reduced risk of death (HR, 0.72; 95% CI, 0.63–0.83; P < 
.001) and greater reductions in progression (HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.69–0.87; 
P < .001), locoregional failure (HR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.66–0.94; P = .007), 
and distant failure (HR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.45–0.89; P = .009).334

of these patients are effectively treated and cured with total laryngectomy 
for progressive disease/recurrence. Yet, even in this setting, the utilization 
of induction chemotherapy has decreased with time. Randomized trials 
and related meta-analyses indicated that concurrent systemic therapy/RT 
(with high-dose cisplatin being the best-studied agent and regimen) 
offered superior locoregional tumor control and OS compared to RT 
alone,288,291-293,295,297,298,300,301 and shorter duration of therapy compared to 
induction therapy followed by radiation. Meta-analyses reported that 
concurrent systemic therapy/RT was more efficacious than an induction 
chemotherapy followed by definitive RT strategy.299,323 In the larynx 
preservation setting, the Intergroup 91-11 trial compared RT alone, 
concurrent cisplatin/RT, and induction cisplatin/fluorouracil followed by RT; 
all arms offered surgery for locally relapsed/refractory disease. The 
concurrent cisplatin/RT arm had the highest larynx preservation rate (see 
Cancer of the Larynx in this Discussion).324 Long-term follow-up of the 
91-11 trial confirmed that concomitant systemic therapy/RT improved the 
larynx preservation rate and that induction chemotherapy followed by RT 
was not superior to RT alone.318 However, OS did not differ among the 
three treatment arms. 

Whether adding induction chemotherapy to concurrent chemoradiation 
(vs. RT alone) results in a clear advantage in OS continues to be 
unclear.335-337 Both the DeCIDE and the PARADIGM phase III trials did not 
show a survival advantage with the incorporation of induction 
chemotherapy followed by concurrent chemoradiation.336,337 In patients 
with stage III or IV SCCHN, a randomized phase II study compared 
induction TPF followed by concurrent cisplatin/fluorouracil and RT versus 
concurrent cisplatin/fluorouracil and RT alone. A higher radiologic 
complete response rate was reported with the incorporation of induction 
chemotherapy.338 Results from a larger follow-up study suggest a survival 
advantage.339 

Other induction chemotherapy regimens have been evaluated in phase II 
trials. The ECOG-ACRIN trial (E2303) showed promising results in terms 

Nonetheless, interest in the role of induction chemotherapy endured for 
several reasons. First, advances in surgery, RT, and concurrent systemic 
therapy/RT have yielded improvements in locoregional control; thus, the 
role of distant metastases as a source of disease progression has 
increased, and induction chemotherapy is a strategy that may reduce the 
risk of distant metastases.325,326 Second, clinicians have increasing 
concern regarding the long-term morbidity of concurrent systemic 
therapy/RT, and thus have an interest in exploring alternative approaches 
that might have a more favorable long-term side effect profile.327 Finally, a 
more effective triplet induction chemotherapy regimen was identified 
compared to the standard cisplatin/fluorouracil used in the induction trials

delivered concurrently with RT following induction TPF.346 

Results of the phase III GORTEC 2007-02 trial, in which 370 patients with 
bulky nodal disease (N2b, N2c, or N3) were randomized to receive 
carboplatin/fluorouracil with RT or TPF followed by cetuximab/RT, showed 
no significant differences between the study arms for survival outcomes 
and local control.347 There was a trend towards a lower rate of distant 
metastases in the TPF arm (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.30–0.99; P = .05).

carboplatin as induction chemotherapy, followed by concurrent systemic 
therapy/RT with the same drug regimen in patients with stage III or IV 
SCCHN (N = 74),340 but the benefit of induction chemotherapy requires 
validation using a randomized design. Two phase II studies evaluated the 
feasibility of TPF with cetuximab followed by concurrent systemic 
therapy/RT or RT alone.341,342 The DeLOS-II trial showed that TPF 
followed by RT, with cetuximab administered throughout, was feasible but 
not superior to TPF and subsequent RT without cetuximab.341 An EORTC 
trial evaluating this induction regimen followed by concurrent systemic 
therapy/RT was stopped prematurely due to numerous serious adverse 
events.342 

The Panel recommends cetuximab administered concurrently with RT 
following induction chemotherapy only in select circumstances, such as in 
patients who are cisplatin-ineligible. Low-dose weekly cisplatin with RT 
following induction chemotherapy is a category 2B option, based on 
extrapolation.336,344 However, because of acute toxicity concerns, 
high-dose cisplatin (100 mg/m2 every 21 days × 3 doses) is not 
recommended with RT after induction cisplatin-based chemotherapy.335,344 

There is a lack of consensus regarding the most appropriate concurrent 
systemic therapy/RT regimen to be administered following induction 
chemotherapy.343 Panel members agree that weekly carboplatin is a 
reasonable agent to use with RT in patients previously treated with 
induction chemotherapy.336 Intent-to-treat analyses from the randomized 
phase II TREMPLIN study showed no significant difference in larynx 
preservation rate at 3 months in patients with locally advanced larynx or 
hypopharynx cancers who received either cisplatin (95%) or cetuximab 
(93%) with RT following induction TPF.344 Although surgery for persistent 
disease was feasible only in patients who received cetuximab with RT 
following TPF, rate of treatment failure was lower in patients who received 
cisplatin with RT. Long-term results of this trial showed no significant 
differences between the study arms for 5-year OS, locoregional control, 
and laryngo-esophageal dysfunction-free survival.345 There were also no 
significant differences in toxicities, although late toxicities tended to be 
more common in the cetuximab arm, compared to the cisplatin arm 
(96.1% vs. 86.2% respectively; P = .10). A randomized phase III 
noninferiority trial showed no differences in PFS, overall response rates 

The data summarized in this section highlights overarching concerns that 
any efficacy gains of a strategy of induction chemotherapy followed by RT 
may be offset by the poorer patient adherence with the RT-based part of 
treatment and the alternative option of shorter duration, better tolerated, 
and at least equally effective concurrent systemic therapy/RT regimens. 
Because of these uncertainties, enrollment of patients in appropriate 
clinical trials of induction chemotherapy is encouraged. Outside of a 
clinical trial, concurrent systemic therapy/RT—with high-dose cisplatin 
preferred—is considered the gold standard by many NCCN Panel 
Members (see Principles of Systemic Therapy for Non-Nasopharyngeal 
Cancers in the algorithm).139-142,288,348 When induction chemotherapy is 
used, data show that the addition of a taxane to cisplatin/fluorouracil (of 
which TPF is the most extensively studied) is more efficacious than 
cisplatin/fluorouracil.334,343 Therefore, when used as induction 
chemotherapy for SCCHN, docetaxel with cisplatin/infusional fluorouracil

respectively. OS favored the pembrolizumab group over the control 
group but did not reach the pre-specified significance threshold at the

Perioperative or Adjuvant Immunotherapy 
The results of two pivotal randomized trials that were conducted in 
patients with resectable or resected locally advanced SCCHN were 
reported in 2025 and 2026: the KEYNOTE-689 and NIVOPOSTOP 
phase III trials. 

As a result of the consistent benefit across the PD-L1–expressing 
subgroups, the FDA approved neoadjuvant pembrolizumab followed by 
adjuvant pembrolizumab/RT followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab as a 
new treatment approach for patients with resectable, PD-L1–positive 
(CPS ≥1), locally advanced SCCHN. The Panel recommends this 
regimen for PD-L1–positive (CPS ≥1) stage III–IVA cancers of the oral 
cavity (other recommended), oropharynx (p16-negative only), 
hypopharynx, and larynx (useful in certain circumstances). For patients 
with ENE and/or positive margins, cisplatin should be added to adjuvant 
pembrolizumab/RT. 

Additional analyses of KEYNOTE-689 data showed that EFS favored the 
pembrolizumab group over the control group across post-surgical high- 
and low-risk pathological subgroups. Fewer participants in the 
pembrolizumab group had high-risk pathological features in the surgical 
specimen and fewer were treated with intensified adjuvant therapy 
(cisplatin + higher dose of RT). The pembrolizumab group was 
associated with a lower rate of distant metastases but a similar rate of 
locoregional failure. Major or complete pathological responses to 
neoadjuvant pembrolizumab correlated with better EFS. However, 
irrespective of pathological response, EFS was numerically better in the 
pembrolizumab group versus the control group. 

The KEYNOTE-689 open-label phase III trial investigated the addition of 
perioperative (neoadjuvant and adjuvant) pembrolizumab to standard of 
care (surgery and adjuvant radiotherapy with or without concomitant 
cisplatin) in 714 patients with resectable locally advanced HNSCC.352 
Baseline characteristics were similar between the two groups. Over 95% 
of patients had HPV-negative disease and tumor PD-L1 CPS ≥1. A 
similar proportion of patients in each group underwent surgery and 
received adjuvant RT-based therapy. At the first interim analysis, the 
median follow-up was 38.3 months. Among participants with PD-L1 CPS 
≥10, event-free survival (EFS) at 36 months assessed by blinded 
independent central review was 59.8% with the pembrolizumab group 
versus 45.9% in the control group (HR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.49–0.88; P = 
.004). In those with PD-L1 CPS ≥1, EFS at 36 months was 58.2% in the 
pembrolizumab group and 44.9% in the control group (HR, 0.70; 95% CI, 
0.55–0.89; P = .003). Among the total population, EFS at 36 months was 
57.6% in the pembrolizumab group and 46.4% in the control group (HR, 
0.73; 95% CI, 0.58–0.92; P = .008). Pathological response in the surgical 
specimen, assessed by blinded independent pathologic review, occurred 
in patients in the pembrolizumab group but not the control group. Major 
pathological response occurred in 13.7% of patients in the CPS ≥10 
population, 9.8% in the CPS ≥1 population, and 9.3% in the total

Principles of Supportive Care 

Nutrition 

The Principles of Nutrition: Management and Supportive Care section in 
the algorithm outlines nutritional management and supportive care for 
patients with H&N cancers who are prone to weight loss, which can often 
be severe, as a result of treatment-related toxicity, disease, and health 
behaviors such as poor nutritional habits.356,357 Patients with H&N cancers 
are also at risk for dehydration. The multidisciplinary expertise of a 
registered dietitian and a speech-language/swallowing therapist should be 
utilized throughout the continuum of care. 

The open-label phase III NIVOPOSTOP trial investigated the addition of 
adjuvant nivolumab to standard-of-care adjuvant high-dose cisplatin/RT in 
666 patients with resected, locally advanced SCCHN of the oral cavity, 
oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx with high-risk adverse pathological 
risk features (positive margin, extracapsular nodal extension, multiple 
perineural invasion, and/or ≥4 positive neck nodes).353 Baseline 
characteristics were similar between arms. Ninety-five percent of patients 
had HPV-negative disease and 86% to 89% had PD-L1 CPS ≥1 disease. 
A similar proportion of patients in each arm (94%) were treated with 
adjuvant cisplatin/RT. Median follow-up was 30.3 months. The 3-year DFS 
assessed by the investigator was 63.1% (95% CI, 57.0%–68.7%) in the 
nivolumab + cisplatin/RT arm versus 52.5% (95% CI, 46.2%–58.4%) in the 
control arm (HR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.60–0.98; P = .034). The locoregional 
recurrence rate was lower in the nivolumab + cisplatin/RT arm; however, 
distant metastases rates were similar between arms. OS favored the 
nivolumab group over the control group, but the number of death events 
were not mature, and the OS outcomes did not reach the pre-specified 
significance threshold at the first analysis; follow-up for survival is ongoing. 
Some TRAEs (including renal disorders, dysphagia, and thyroid disorders) 
were more frequent and severe in the nivolumab + cisplatin/RT arm. 

The phase II, open-label, nonrandomized OPTIMA II trial evaluated the 
addition of nivolumab to neoadjuvant nab-paclitaxel and carboplatin 
followed by response-adapted locoregional therapy in 73 patients with 
HPV-positive locoregionally advanced oropharyngeal cancer.354 Deep 
response rate in the nivolumab group was 70.8% (95% CI, 58.9%–81.3%), 
which did not statistically differ from the historical control group from the 
first OPTIMA trial (nab-paclitaxel and carboplatin alone).355 The 2-year 
PFS and OS were 90.0% (95% CI, 0.80–0.95) and 91.4% (95% CI, 0.82–
0.96), respectively. 

Patients who have had significant weight loss (5% body weight loss over 1 
month, or 10% body weight loss over 6 months) and/or difficulty 
swallowing due to pain or tumor involvement require nutritional evaluation 
and close monitoring of their weight to prevent further weight loss.358,359 In 
addition, all patients should receive nutritional evaluation before and after 
treatment to assess the need for interventions (eg, enteral support via 
feeding tubes).360,361 Lymphedema of the H&N commonly occurs in 
patients and is associated with increased symptom burden (eg, negative 
cosmetic impact, trouble breathing, swallow dysfunction, and pain).362-364 
Fibrosis can also occur.365 As lymphedema and fibrosis negatively impact 
function and QOL, prompt identification and treatment are essential given 
the progressive nature of lymphedema and potential complications. 
Approximately 3 in 4 cases of lymphedema are diagnosed within 3 years 
of treatment; however, it can develop anytime in the life of the survivor. 
Early detection/diagnosis and early referral are key for optimal 
lymphedema management because stages 0 and 1 are reversible, 
whereas stages 2 and 3 are less responsive to treatment. Patient referrals 
to occupational therapy to learn massage techniques (eg, lymphatic 
decompression therapy) or to be fitted for custom-made compression 
devices may be warranted. Patients are also at risk for problems with 
speech and/or swallowing. Treatment and/or the progression of their

369 Evaluation by a speech-language/swallowing therapist is needed 
before, during, and after treatment to help mitigate potential problems.370-

372 Patients are also at risk for dental problems (see Principles of 
Oral/Dental Evaluation and Management in the algorithm). Long-term 
swallowing and dental dysfunction are particular risks that are worsened 
by multimodality therapy and require long-term specialized attention. 

Oral mucositis, or tissue damage, is common in patients treated with RT 
for H&N cancers,373-378 although use of advanced RT techniques (eg, 
IMRT) may decrease the incidence and duration of this damage.373,379,380 
Oral mucositis causes pain in the mouth, which may affect the ability to eat 
and drink.373,376,377,381 Oral mucositis may be associated with breaks and/or 
delays in treatment, as well as hospitalization.374,375,377 Oral mucositis is 
more severe in patients receiving concurrent systemic therapy/RT.377 The 
Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer and the 
International Society of Oral Oncology have published clinical practice 
guidelines for treatment of oral mucositis, although there are few high-
quality studies in this area.382,383 Prevention and management of mucositis 
constitute an unmet medical need. 

were randomized to receive gabapentin or usual care.385 Patients 
randomized to receive gabapentin reported a greater reduction in pain, 
compared to patients randomized to receive usual care (P = .004). A small 
retrospective study including patients with H&N cancer treated with RT or 
systemic therapy/RT showed that treatment with gabapentin for pain from 
oral mucositis is associated with a reduced need for narcotic pain 
medication and high doses of opioids.376 A single-institution study 
demonstrated that very-high-dose prophylactic gabapentin (2700 mg daily) 
also reduced the number of patients requiring narcotics.386 An unplanned 
secondary analysis of two consecutive prospective clinical trials showed 
that high-dose prophylactic gabapentin (3600 mg daily) was associated 
with greater time to first use of opioids, compared to 900 mg daily (P < 
.001).387 A phase 2 randomized trial showed that over 90% of patients 
tolerated prophylactic gabapentin (3600 mg daily) well, though the addition 
of venlafaxine did not result in improvements in pain control.388 The toxicity 
of large dosages should not be underestimated and was not adequately 
explored in these studies. Larger scale studies are awaited to fully assess 
the generalizability and toxicity of this dosing schedule. In a randomized, 
double-blind, placebo-controlled study from China (N = 128), patients with 
RT-related neuropathic pain who received pregabalin reported greater 
pain relief (P = .006 for 30% pain relief and P = .003 for 50% pain relief) 
and greater pain intensity reduction (P = .003) than patients who received 
a placebo.389 The Panel recommends consideration of doxepin, 
diphenhydramine-lidocaine-antacid mouthwash, pregabalin (category 2B), 
or gabapentin for pain related to oral mucositis, as clinically indicated and 
as tolerated. 

In the randomized phase III Alliance A221304 trial, patients with H&N 
cancer who were treated with RT (N = 275) were randomized to receive a 
diphenhydramine-lidocaine-antacid mouthwash, doxepin mouthwash, or a 
placebo.384 The reduction in mucositis pain during the first 4 hours of 
treatment was significantly greater in the patients who received the 
diphenhydramine-lidocaine-antacid mouthwash (P = .004) or the doxepin 
mouthwash (P = .02), compared to the placebo. The practicality and 
effectiveness of the doxepin-based regimen through an entire course of 
RT is not established. Gabapentin is also under investigation for treatment 
of pain from oral mucositis. In a prospective randomized pilot study, 
patients with H&N cancer who were treated with chemoradiation (N = 79) 

NCCN Panel members agree that reactive feeding tube placement, in 
which patients are first given oral nutrition supplements, followed by 
enteral feeding, when maintenance of nutritional requirements is no longer 
possible, is appropriate in selected patients with H&N cancers,357 such as 
those in which tumors or mucositis interfere with swallowing function.390

tumor cells as it passes through the tumor site. 

Oral/Dental Evaluation and Management 

Reactive feeding tube placement should be considered if at least two of 
the following criteria are met: inability to maintain adequate intake (ie, 
<60% of estimated energy expenditure) for >10 days; >5% weight loss in a 
single month; severe mucositis, odynophagia, dysphagia, or aspiration; or 
older age (ie, >60 years).391 A retrospective analysis including 100 patients 
treated with chemoradiation for advanced SCCHN showed that age >60 
years was the most significant risk factor predicting need for enteral 
feeding (P = .003).392 

Patients with H&N cancers are at risk of oral and dental complications 
after surgery or RT because of treatment-induced xerostomia and salivary 
gland dysfunction, which are associated with increased dental caries and 
its sequelae, including dentoalveolar infection and 
osteoradionecrosis.369,373,377,395-399 In addition, RT to the salivary and oral 
soft tissues is also associated with bone demineralization and trismus of 
the masticatory muscles. Radiation-related caries and other dental hard 
tissue changes can appear within the first 3 months following RT. Using 
IMRT and limiting the RT dose to the salivary glands and oral cavity have 
been shown to decrease xerostomia and damage to the teeth.395,396,400-406 
Dental/oral evaluation and management can help decrease dental caries 
and associated problems such as dentoalveolar infection and 
osteoradionecrosis.373,377,399,400,406-415 

There is no consensus about whether prophylactic tube placement is 
appropriate. Advantages of prophylactic tube placement include 
reductions in hospitalizations and treatment-related weight loss, as well as 
improved QOL.393 However, this practice is also associated with 
disadvantages, such as longer dependence on feeding tubes and worse 
long-term functional outcomes, compared to a reactive approach.393 The 
NCCN Guidelines provide recommendations for prophylactic tube 
placement, which should be strongly considered in select patients (eg, 
those with severe pretreatment weight loss, ongoing dehydration or 
dysphagia, significant comorbidities, severe aspiration risk, anticipated 
swallowing issues).357,359 In patients with adequate swallowing function, 
care must be given with the help of speech and language pathologists to 
ensure that patients continue to swallow to prevent severe fibrosis and 
permanent feeding tube dependence (see Principles of Nutrition: 
Management and Supportive Care in the algorithm). With swallowing 
therapy, adequate pain control, and access to IV fluids, feeding tubes can 
be avoided in most patients. The NCCN Guidelines do not recommend 
prophylactic tube placement in patients with lower risk disease (ie, those 
without significant pretreatment weight loss, significant aspiration, or 
severe dysphagia), although these patients’ weights should be carefully 
monitored during and after treatment. Tumor implantation of the stoma is a 
rare complication of gastronomy tube placement.394 Although the exact 

The recommended dental/oral evaluations before, during, and after RT are 
described in detail in the algorithm and are summarized here. A dental/oral 
treatment plan needs to be implemented before RT and should include the 
following: 1) eliminating potential sources of infection; 2) if performing 
dental extractions, allowing adequate time for healing before RT; 3) 
treating active dental caries and periodontal disease; 4) treating oral 
candidiasis; and 5) educating patients about preventive strategies, 
including the elimination of sugar-based candies or gum for dry mouth 
prevention.399,416 Some of the general strategies to decrease oral and 
dental complications include: 1) decrease dry mouth (eg, by increasing 
hydration and using salivary substitutes; gustatory stimulation with xylitol 
lozenges or discs that adhere to the gums, teeth, or dentures; cholinergic 
agonists such as pilocarpine and cevimeline; and the minimization of 
alcohol and caffeine consumption)417-419; 2) reduce risk of dental caries

is common (50%–60%) in patients with anterior (oral) tongue cancers. 
The incidence of lymph node metastases in cancer of the mucosal lip 
(especially early-stage lower lip) is historically low based on AJCC 7th 
edition staging,426 averaging <10%, with higher rates seen in T3/4 
disease or with oral commissure involvement. With the incorporation of 
depth of invasion into T staging in the AJCC 8th edition,43 it has become 
the primary determinant of occult nodal risk and should guide 
management of the clinically N0 neck. Lesions with depth of invasion 
>10 mm are upstaged and generally warrant elective regional nodal

dentoalveolar infection (eg, with frequent evaluations to detect and treat 
disease promptly); 4) prevent and address osteoradionecrosis; 5) 
decrease trismus of the masticatory muscles (eg, by using custom mouth-
opening devices to maintain range of motion)421-423; 6) Candidiasis 
prevention and control; and 7) have patient undergo evaluations during 
and after treatment to help minimize complications.399,417,418,424 
Submandibular gland transfer is an approach that may be used in select 
circumstances to prevent xerostomia,425 but the Panel does not endorse 
this approach due to lack of evidence and the availability of other options 
for xerostomia prevention and management. Major dental work such as 
extractions can be problematic for an irradiated mandible. Therefore, any 
planned procedures should be performed by dentists well-acquainted with 
this treatment setting and potential related morbidities, and in consultation 
with the treating radiation oncologist. 

Cancers of the lip mucosa are now staged as oral cavity cancers (see 
Table 1). The AJCC TNM staging system reflects tumor size, extension, 
and nodal disease.43 In the 8th edition of the AJCC Cancer Staging 
Manual, cancers of the external vermilion lip are staged as cutaneous 
carcinomas of the H&N, due to their similarity to skin cancers excluding 
melanoma.43 For treatment guidance, see the NCCN Guidelines for 
Squamous Cell Skin Cancer (available at www.NCCN.org). 

Workup 

During and after treatment, the goals of dental/oral management include: 
1) addressing xerostomia; 2) preventing trismus; and 3) detecting and 
treating oral candidiasis.377,399,416 Additional goals after treatment include: 
1) preventing and treating dental caries; 2) surveying the mouth for early 
signs of post-radiation osteonecrosis; and 3) preventing oral 
candidiasis.377,399,416 

Cancer of the Oral Cavity (Including Mucosal Lip) 

Imaging to assess mandibular involvement and regional nodal disease, 
along with a thorough dental evaluation is particularly important for staging 
(see Table 1) and treatment planning in oral cavity cancers. A complete 
H&N examination, biopsy, and other studies (see Cancer of the Oral 
Cavity [Including Mucosal Lip]: Workup in the algorithm) are also 
recommended. For patients likely to receive RT (primary or adjuvant), 
pretreatment dental evaluation and ongoing dental care are critical to 
minimize the risk of osteoradionecrosis. Nutrition, speech, and swallowing 
evaluations are recommended for select patients (see Principles of 
Nutrition: Management and Supportive Care in the algorithm). 

The oral cavity includes the buccal mucosa, upper and lower alveolar 
ridges, retromolar trigone, floor of mouth, hard palate, and the anterior 
two-thirds of the tongue. It has a rich lymphatic network, with initial 
regional spread typically occurring to lymph nodes in levels I through III. 
Regional node involvement at presentation is evident in approximately 
30% of patients, but the risk varies by subsite. The risk of lymph node 
metastases is influenced by location, size, tumor thickness, depth of 
invasion, and tumor grade. For example, primaries of the alveolar ridge

is low, routine inclusion of levels IV and V is not indicated in the N0 setting 
in the absence of specific high-risk features. Therefore, the extent of 
dissection (specifically the benefit of routinely including levels IV and V) in 
the N0 setting remains uncertain.429 In contrast, the benefit of elective 
neck dissection itself is well established. A randomized trial demonstrated 
improved OS and DFS with elective neck dissection compared with 
observation in patients with early-stage oral cavity cancer.430 These 
findings are supported by subsequent meta-analyses and a Cochrane 
review, and elective neck dissection is standard practice in appropriately 
selected patients.103,431 

Treatment is based on clinical stage, patient medical status, anticipated 
functional and cosmetic outcomes, and patient preference. For resectable 
oral cavity cancers, surgery is the standard of care and provides superior 
locoregional control compared with nonsurgical approaches. Most small or 
superficial cancers can be resected without significant functional or 
cosmetic impact, and, for more advanced disease, microvascular 
reconstruction reliably permits oncologically appropriate resection without 
prohibitive functional compromise. Multidisciplinary team involvement is 
essential given the impact on mastication, swallowing, and speech. 

Elective neck dissection in early-stage mucosal lip cancer remains 
controversial. Early-stage mucosal lip cancers have a low baseline risk of 
nodal metastasis. Elective neck dissection is not routinely required but 
should be performed in selected patients with high-risk features. Depth of 
invasion thresholds used for other oral cavity subsites cannot be assumed 
to apply uniformly to mucosal lip and should be interpreted cautiously, as 
depth of invasion has not specifically been examined in mucosal lip 
tumors.432 Nonetheless, a depth >4 mm or T2 classification, oral 
commissure involvement, or advanced T stage may justify elective 
supraomohyoid dissection, with special attention to submental and 
perifacial nodes. 

RT is equally effective for early-stage mucosal lip cancer. A nonsurgical 
approach may also be considered when surgical morbidity is high (eg, 
total glossectomy) or when the patient prefers organ preservation, though 
systemic therapy with radiation is generally considered less effective for 
locoregional control compared with upfront surgery. Definitive RT may be 
offered to patients who are medically inoperable, decline surgery,427 or 
need local control in incurable cases. Postoperative radiation is 
recommended based on pathological findings and disease stage. 
Treatment decisions are informed by TN stage and the risk of nodal 
involvement in N0 disease (see Cancer of the Oral Cavity [Including 
Mucosal Lip] in the algorithm). 

Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) may also be considered in selected 
high-risk cases. SLNB can identify occult cervical metastases (see 
Principles of Surgery in the algorithm).433-439 While early-stage lip cancers 
rarely have occult nodal disease, SLNB is feasible in patients at high risk 
based on tumor size and depth.440-442 A systematic review of 98 studies 
showed sensitivity and specificity of 82.7% and 98.1%, respectively, for 
detecting cervical metastases in cT1–2 N0 cancers.443 In a phase III 
multicenter RCT (n = 307), SLNB and elective neck dissection showed no 
significant differences in recurrence-free survival, DSS, or OS.444 A meta-

For early-stage oral cavity cancers, the preferred initial treatment is 
surgical resection of the primary tumor. Most patients undergo ipsilateral 
or bilateral neck dissection, guided by factors such as depth of invasion, 
proximity to the midline, and tumor location (see Head and Neck Surgery: 
Neck Dissection above). A depth of invasion >3 mm warrants elective 
neck dissection.428 This threshold reliably identifies patients at sufficient 
risk of occult nodal metastasis. Observation is appropriate only for 
carefully selected patients with depth of invasion <3 mm and no additional 
high-risk features. Although the risk of occult metastasis to levels IV and V

Radiation Therapy 
RT should be delivered according to Principles of Radiation Therapy in the 
NCCN Guidelines, with dose and volume determined by risk category. For 
definitive RT in T1–2, N0 disease, doses to intermediate and low-risk sites 
range from 54 Gy (2.0 Gy/fraction) to 63 Gy (1.6 Gy/fraction). Suspected 
subclinical disease sites may receive 54–60 Gy in sequential IMRT, or 54–
63 Gy in IMRT with dose painting, depending on fraction size (1.6–1.8 
Gy). Doses of 66–70 Gy are appropriate for high-risk disease. 

analysis of 12 trials also found no differences in OS, DFS, or recurrence 
between SLNB and elective neck dissection, and confirmed SLNB’s non-
inferiority regarding DSS.445 However, the evidence was of low quality, 
supporting the need for further RCTs. Results from an ongoing NRG trial 
(Clinical trial ID: NCT04333537) may provide additional clarity. Although 
agents like technetium Tc99m tilmanocept have been evaluated for SLNB 
in oral cancers,446,447 the data are insufficient for the Panel to recommend 
a specific agent. SLNB is an acceptable alternative to elective neck 
dissection in experienced centers with established protocols, as outcomes 
are operator dependent. Elective neck dissection remains the reference 
standard. 

RT may include EBRT with or without brachytherapy depending on tumor 
size. Brachytherapy should only be performed at experienced centers and 
may be appropriate in select cases (eg, close/positive margins after 
resection and flap reconstruction). While supportive data are limited, 
NCCN provides guidance on both low- and high-dose rate 
brachytherapy.448,449 

Follow-up/Surveillance 

Surveillance recommendations are provided in the algorithm (see Follow-
up Recommendations in the algorithm). 

Cancer of the Oropharynx 

Postsurgical adjuvant treatment depends on the presence of adverse 
pathologic features. Positive or close margins and ENE are high-risk 
features and indications for systemic therapy with radiation (category 1). 
Perineural, vascular, and lymphatic invasion are less established 
indications but typically warrant adjuvant radiation alone. Concurrent 
systemic therapy should be considered in selected patients with multiple 
intermediate risk factors. Patients with ENE with or without positive 
mucosal margins should receive postoperative systemic therapy/RT 
(category 1). Re-resection is preferred for positive or close margins when 
technically feasible prior to adjuvant therapy; if not feasible, adjuvant 
therapy is appropriate. 

The oropharynx includes the base of the tongue, tonsils, soft palate, and 
pharyngeal wall. The base of tongue and tonsils, anatomical subsites rich 
in tonsillar lymphoid tissue, are recognized as hotspots for HPV-
associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC), while the 
soft palate and pharyngeal wall are characterized as typically non-tonsillar 
regions of the oropharynx, keratinizing, and HPV-independent.450 
Depending on the subsite involved, 15% to 75% of patients present with 
lymph node involvement. 

For resected advanced-stage cancers with ENE and/or positive mucosal 
margins, systemic therapy/RT (category 1) is recommended.139-142,144 Re-
resection for positive or close margins is more complex following free flap 
reconstruction. EBRT should be considered; the role of brachytherapy 
remains underexplored (see Radiation Therapy below). For other high-risk 
features (eg, pT3/4, pN2/3, level IV/V nodes, perineural, vascular, or 
lymphatic invasion), RT alone is recommended, or systemic therapy/RT 
may be considered.

A multidisciplinary consultation is encouraged including a registered 
dietitian and a speech-language/swallowing therapist as clinically indicated 
(see Principles of Nutrition: Management and Supportive Care in the 
algorithm). Accurate staging (see Table 3 for p16-negative oropharyngeal 
cancer and Table 4 for p16-positive oropharyngeal cancer) depends on a 
complete H&N examination and appropriate cross-sectional imaging 
studies (see Cancer of the Oropharynx: Workup in algorithm).43,451

individual patient data analysis including 13 cohorts of patients from 
Canada and Europe (N = 7654) showed that patients with discordant p16 
expression and HPV status (5-year OS of 53.2%; 95% CI, 46.6%–60.8% 
for p16-negative/HPV-positive; 5-year OS of 54.7%; 95% CI, 49.2%–
