Maxillary Sinus Tumors 

chemotherapy.656 This was followed by a response-directed approach to 
locoregional treatment (chemoradiation versus surgery). 

Systemic therapy should routinely be part of the overall treatment for 
patients with SNUC with neuroendocrine features; small cell, high-grade 
olfactory esthesioneuroblastoma; midline NUT; or SNEC histologies. The 
optimal regimen for these patients is not well-defined, but typically 
regimens used for high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas (eg, etoposide 
plus platinum, cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin/vincristine) or for advanced 
SCCHN (eg, TPF, PF, TP) are used.657-666 After curative-intent treatment, 
long-term follow-up is necessary for esthesioneuroblastoma, since late 
recurrences can occur even after 15 years.665,667,668 

Surgical resection followed by postoperative radiotherapy remains a 
cornerstone of treatment for most maxillary sinus tumors, except limited-
extent T1–2 tumors resected with negative margins (see Maxillary Sinus 
Tumors in the algorithm).673-676 The principles are generally similar to those 
described above for ethmoid sinus tumors. For patients with SNUC with 
neuroendocrine features; small cell, high-grade olfactory 
esthesioneuroblastoma; or midline NUT or SNEC histologies, systemic 
therapy should be routinely included as part of the treatment plan (see 
Ethmoid Sinus Tumors in this Discussion). Participation in clinical trials is 
recommended for patients with malignant tumors of the paranasal sinuses 
with these histologies. 

RT fractionation for patients with maxillary sinus tumors is described in 
Maxillary Sinus Tumors: Principles of Radiation Therapy in the algorithm. 
Studies using IMRT have shown that it reduces the incidence of 
complications, such as radiation-induced ophthalmic toxicity, although the 
5-year OS rate was not improved.235,675,677-680 Similar to the 
recommendation for ethmoid sinus tumors, IMRT or PBT is recommended 
in this anatomical area due to proximity to the visual structures and proton 
therapy is preferred if the normal tissue constraints cannot be met by 
IMRT. 

Induction chemotherapy is an option for patients with newly diagnosed T3, 
T4a disease, and options are based on molecular features. In a single-
center retrospective study including 95 patients with SNUC, concurrent 
systemic therapy/RT following complete or partial response to induction 
chemotherapy (ie, etoposide with platinum-based therapy) was associated 
with a 5-year DSS rate of 81% (95% CI, 69%–88%), compared to 59% 
(95% CI, 53%–66%) for the entire sample.669 The DSS rate for patients 
who received surgery with adjuvant therapy following a less than partial 
response to induction chemotherapy was 39% (95% CI, 30%–46%). 
Definitive trials of induction chemotherapy prior to surgery are currently 
underway within the U.S. cooperative groups. 

Follow-up 

Recommendations for surveillance are provided in the algorithm (see 
Follow-up Recommendations in the algorithm). 

Very Advanced Head and Neck Cancers 

The algorithms for very advanced H&N cancers include: 1) newly 
diagnosed (M0) locally advanced T4b, N0–3, or newly diagnosed 
unresectable regional nodal disease, or those unfit for surgery; 2) 
metastatic disease at initial presentation (M1); or 3) recurrent or persistent 

For patients with metastatic disease, options include platinum combined 
with etoposide (with or without concurrent RT)657,670,671 and 
cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin/vincristine (category 2B). While there 
remains no known effective treatment for metastatic midline NUT 
carcinoma, there are targeted therapies such as bromodomain inhibitors 
under active investigation.645,672 Because of a paucity of data concerning 
the use of systemic therapies, appropriate use of other systemic options, 
including immunotherapy, remains undefined.

cure for patients with newly diagnosed locoregional but unresectable 
disease. For recurrent disease, the goal is cure if surgery or radiation 
remains feasible, or palliation if the patient has received previous RT and 
the disease is unresectable. For patients with hematogenous metastases, 
the goal is palliation and survival prolongation.

chemoradiation options include carboplatin/paclitaxel (category 2B based 
on less Panel consensus), weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m2, and docetaxel (for 
patients not eligible for cisplatin).145,305,682-684 Category 2B chemoradiation 
options that the Panel has deemed useful only in select circumstances are 
infusional fluorouracil/hydroxyurea, cisplatin with infusional fluorouracil, 
and cisplatin/paclitaxel.685,686 

Treatment 

The treatment of patients with unresectable locoregional, persistent, 
recurrent, or metastatic H&N cancers is dictated by the patient’s PS and 
intent of treatment (ie, palliative vs. curative). Patients with good PS may 
tolerate a wide range of treatment options, whereas patients with reduced 
PS cannot. 

Other options for patients with a PS of 2–4 are described in the algorithm 
[see Very Advanced Head and Neck Cancer: Treatment of Newly 
Diagnosed (M0) T4b, N0–3 or Unresectable Primary or Nodal Disease or 
Unfit for Surgery in the algorithm]. Primary systemic therapy/RT regimens 
are listed in the Principles of Systemic Therapy for Non-Nasopharyngeal 
Cancers in the algorithm. RT fractionation for patients with newly 
diagnosed, very advanced disease is described in the Very Advanced 
Head and Neck Cancers: Principles of Radiation Therapy in the NCCN 
algorithm. 

Metastatic Disease 
For patients with metastatic (M1) disease at initial presentation, enrollment 
in a clinical trial is preferred. Palliative adjunctive measures include RT, 
surgery, analgesics, and other therapies to control manifestations of 
disease spread (eg, pain, hypercalcemia, malnutrition). Locoregional 
treatment (eg, surgery, RT, ablative therapies) may be used for 
oligometastatic disease.687-689 

Newly Diagnosed Locoregionally Advanced Disease 
In patients with a PS of 0 or 1, the recommended treatment of newly 
diagnosed, very advanced disease is concurrent systemic therapy/RT, 
with a large amount of phase III data supporting high-dose cisplatin as a 
category 1 preferred recommendation (see Systemic Therapy for Locally 
Advanced Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck in this 
Discussion).288,318 There are also considerable phase III data from Europe 
that support the use of carboplatin/fluorouracil with concurrent RT.191 This 
treatment is also considered a category 1 preferred option. Cisplatin-
based induction systemic therapy has been studied, followed by RT alone 
or chemoradiation with weekly platinum or cetuximab.344 However, an 
improvement in OS with the incorporation of induction chemotherapy, 
compared to proceeding directly to state-of-the-art concurrent systemic 
therapy/RT, has not been established in randomized studies.336,337 
Cetuximab with concurrent RT is a category 2B option based on phase II 
and phase III data but is distinctly inferior to cisplatin with concurrent RT, 
particularly in patients with HPV-positive disease, as discussed above 
(see Systemic Therapy for Locally Advanced Squamous Cell Carcinoma 

Historically, single-agent and combination systemic therapy have both 
been used.598 Response rates to single-agent therapies range from 15% 
to 35%.599,690,691 Randomized trials assessing a cisplatin-based 
combination regimen (cisplatin/fluorouracil) versus single-agent therapy 
with cisplatin, fluorouracil, or methotrexate showed significantly higher 
response rates, but no difference in OS and greater toxicity for the 
combination regimen.588,589,592,692,693 Complete response is associated with

longer survival and, although infrequent, has been reported more often 
with combination regimens.589 A phase III randomized trial (EXTREME) of 
442 patients found that cetuximab plus cisplatin/5-FU or 
carboplatin/fluorouracil improved response rate (36% vs. 20%; P < .001) 
and median survival compared to the standard chemotherapy doublet of 
platinum/fluorouracil in a patient population predominantly linked to 
tobacco and alcohol use (10.1 vs. 7.4 months; P = .04).694 A randomized 
phase III trial found no significant difference in survival when comparing 
cisplatin/fluorouracil and cisplatin/paclitaxel.588 A single-arm phase II trial 
(ELAN-FIT) demonstrated that, for patients who are non-frail (fit) and aged 
≥70 years with recurrent or metastatic SCCHN, an adapted EXTREME 
regimen can be used as first-line therapy.695 Clinical outcomes were 
comparable to those previously reported with the standard EXTREME 
regimen or the TPEx (docetaxel, platinum, and cetuximab) regimen in 
younger patient populations. 

Results from KEYNOTE-048 showed that, in patients with a PD-L1 CPS 
of ≥20 or ≥1, median OS was better in patients who received 
pembrolizumab monotherapy, compared to those who received the 
EXTREME regimen (median, 14.9 vs. 10.7 months, respectively; HR, 
0.61; 95% CI, 0.45–0.83; P < .001 for CPS ≥20; median, 12.3 vs. 10.3 
months, respectively; HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.64–0.96; P = .009 for CPS 
≥1).696 In an update with a median study follow-up of 45.0 months, OS 
improved with pembrolizumab in the PD-L1 CPS ≥20 (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 
0.46–0.81) and CPS ≥1 populations (HR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.61–0.89).699 
OS improved with pembrolizumab and chemotherapy in the PD-L1 CPS 
≥20 (HR, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.46–0.84), CPS ≥1 (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.53–
0.78), and total (HR, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.59–0.85) populations. This supports 
CPS ≥1 for pembrolizumab monotherapy, and no PD-L1–based selection 
for combination of chemotherapy and pembrolizumab. No formal 
comparison exists between both pembrolizumab-containing arms, and 
the selection of regimens remains based on clinical judgment. 

More contemporary trials evaluating immune checkpoint inhibitors 
demonstrated efficacy in patients with recurrent or metastatic SCCHN.696-

698 Pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 antibody, was evaluated as a first-line 
option for recurrent or metastatic SCCHN in the KEYNOTE-048 trial (N = 
882).696 Patients were randomized to receive pembrolizumab, 
pembrolizumab with a platinum and fluorouracil, or the EXTREME 
regimen. In the total population, an OS benefit was observed in the 
pembrolizumab/platinum/fluorouracil arm, compared to the EXTREME 
arm (median OS, 13 vs. 10.7 months, respectively; HR, 0.77; 95% CI, 
0.63–0.93; P = .003). PFS, however, did not significantly differ between 
these two study arms. Median duration of response was greater in 
patients treated with pembrolizumab monotherapy or pembrolizumab 
with chemotherapy, compared to patients treated with the EXTREME 
regimen. 

The Panel considers immunotherapy as the preferred first-line systemic 
therapy option for all patients with recurrent, unresectable, or metastatic 
disease who have no surgical or radiotherapeutic option. Specifically, 
pembrolizumab alone (for patients with PD-L1 positive [CPS ≥1]) or 
pembrolizumab/platinum/infusional fluorouracil are both category 1 
preferred first-line options based on the results of KEYNOTE-048; the 
combination regimen may be particularly suitable in patients with a PS of 
0 or 1 and either a large burden of disease or nearing a clinical crisis.696 
Other combination regimens recommended by the Panel for treatment of 
metastatic SCCHN include: 1) cisplatin or carboplatin, plus infusional 
fluorouracil with cetuximab (category 1)694; 2) cisplatin or carboplatin, 
plus a taxane587,588; 3) cisplatin with cetuximab593,700; 4) cisplatin with 
infusional fluorouracil588,589; or 5) cetuximab with a platinum and a 
taxane.700-704 Extrapolating from Guigay et al,704 a taxane can be

Cetuximab combined with an anti–PD-1 antibody (pembrolizumab or 
nivolumab) is also an option for recurrent or metastatic SCCHN based on 
results from non-randomized phase II trials.706,707 Other options that the 
Panel considers useful in certain circumstances are cisplatin/pemetrexed 
(for PS 0–1 only),708 cetuximab with a taxane,700,704,709 
gemcitabine/paclitaxel,710 and nivolumab/ipilimumab (PD-L1 positive 
[CPS ≥20] and first-line only).711 These are all category 2B options 
except for paclitaxel/cetuximab. Single agents recommended by the 
Panel include cisplatin, carboplatin, paclitaxel, docetaxel, infusional 
fluorouracil, methotrexate, capecitabine, and cetuximab.589,592-

Among patients with unresectable recurrence or persistence in a 
previously non-irradiated field, RT with concurrent systemic therapy is 
recommended, with the duration of RT and choice of systemic agent 
dependent on the PS. No randomized data exist that define a preferred 
systemic therapy/RT combination in this setting, although early-phase 
studies have explored carboplatin, PD-1 inhibitors, and cetuximab. In 
situations where patient or tumor factors render patients as poor 
candidates for curative-intent radiation or surgery, the treatment approach 
is the same as that for patients with metastatic disease; however, in the 
absence of distant metastatic disease and/or in the presence of 
symptoms, re-irradiation with systemic therapy is increasingly feasible 
(see below). Locoregional treatment such as palliative radiation may be 
considered in the presence of distant metastasis with locoregional failure 
to alleviate tumor burden-related symptoms. RT fractionation for patients 
with recurrent or persistent disease is described in Very Advanced Head 
and Neck Cancers: Principles of Radiation Therapy in the algorithm). 

Locoregionally Recurrent or Persistent Disease 
A multidisciplinary evaluation is critical in defining appropriate therapy for 
patients with local and/or regional disease recurrence or persistence 
without distant metastasis. A subset of these patients can be approached 
with curative intent local therapy, and the therapeutic options depend on 
several factors, including: type of prior therapy (surgery vs. radiation), 
interval between prior therapy and recurrence, desire for functional 
preservation, and patient PS. 

In general, surgery is recommended for resectable recurrent or persistent 
locoregional disease, in the absence of distant metastatic disease; 
adjuvant therapy depends on pathologic risk factors. Patients with 
resectable recurrent or persistent locoregional disease who have not 
previously been treated with RT may also be treated with concurrent 
systemic therapy/RT (high-dose cisplatin is the preferred [category 1] 
systemic agent).288 Combination systemic therapy followed by RT or 
systemic therapy/RT (category 2B) may be considered for cytoreduction or 

Reirradiation 
Reirradiation may be offered to patients with locally and/or regionally 
recurrent or persistent H&N cancer, using IMRT, PBT, or SBRT. A 
randomized phase III multicenter trial in France (N = 130) showed that 
reirradiation combined with systemic therapy in patients following a 
resected recurrence improves DFS, compared to patients receiving only 
surgery (HR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.13–2.50; P = .01).714 However, the toxicity of 
this regimen was considerable, with grade 3 of 4 acute toxicity 
(mucositis/pharyngitis) in 28% of patients. Results achieved using the 
older techniques in this study may not apply to the current day, with use of 
IMRT becoming routine. As previously stated, SBRT has been 
investigated only in small series and studies.283,284

in one retrospective study of proton therapy reirradiation, three patients 
died (out of 60), possibly due to reirradiation-related effects.727 

When concurrent systemic therapy is given with conventionally 
fractionated reirradiation, cisplatin with concurrent RT is the preferred 
option for individuals with unresectable recurrent or persistent disease 
who received prior RT.143,683 The Panel also recommends carboplatin, 
cetuximab, or docetaxel with concurrent RT as useful in certain 
circumstances as a reirradiation and concurrent systemic therapy option 
(all category 2B).145,309,578,580 

Dosing schedules that may be used for reirradiation are described in 
Radiation Techniques in the algorithm but in general, these schedules are 
similar to those used for initial treatment. Radiation volumes should 
usually include only volumes of known disease, to minimize the amount of 
tissue receiving high doses in previously irradiated regions. Therefore, 
prophylactic treatment (eg, elective nodal irradiation) is not routinely 
indicated.730 There are currently knowledge gaps regarding the 
appropriate use of reirradiation, and patients should be encouraged to 
enroll in clinical trials.622,721 

Disease That Has Progressed on or After Platinum Therapy 
After progression of disease on platinum-based therapy, options are listed 
in the Guidelines (see Principles of Systemic Therapy for Non-
Nasopharyngeal Cancer: Recurrent, Unresectable, or Metastatic in the 
algorithm). Multigene panel testing may be considered to identify 
biomarkers for applicable targeted therapies. 

Advanced RT techniques should be used for reirradiation. A retrospective 
review of 227 patients showed that IMRT-based reirradiation of the H&N 
may be associated with local control and improved survival rates, but 
toxicity rates were considerable, with adverse events grade 3 or higher 
occurring in 16% of patients at 2 years.622,715 Use of concurrent systemic 
therapy may be associated with greater risk of toxicity. Rates for 1-year 
local control, distant control, DFS, and OS were 51%, 90%, 49%, and 
64%, respectively, and adverse events of grade 3 or higher were rare. The 
best outcomes for SBRT in reirradiation are in patients with smaller tumors 
(<25 cc) and no skin involvement.716 Intraoperative RT (IORT) and 
brachytherapy may also be used for select patients at high-volume 
centers.717-719 IORT is usually dosed at 10 to 15 Gy and followed by 40 to 
50 Gy using EBRT preferably IMRT.720 

The decision to treat with reirradiation should take into account surgical 
resectability, comorbidities of the patient, the toxicity of previous treatment 
methods, organ dysfunction, and the amount of time that has passed since 
previous treatment.721-724 Treatment planning should at a minimum take 
brainstem, spinal cord, and laryngeal lifetime dose limits into account so 
that the safest maximum dose is delivered.721,725,726 PBT may be used for 
reirradiation when normal tissue constraints cannot be met by photon-
based therapy.622,727-729 Retrospective studies show that PBT used for 
reirradiation may be associated with good outcomes (eg, 65%–84% OS, 
improved locoregional control, and freedom from distant metastasis as 

Nivolumab was assessed in a phase III RCT including 361 patients with 
recurrent SCCHN whose disease had progressed within 6 months 
following platinum-based chemotherapy.698 With a median follow-up of 
5.1 (range, 0–16.8) months, the OS was significantly greater in patients 
given nivolumab, compared to patients given standard, second-line, 
single-agent systemic therapy (methotrexate, docetaxel, or cetuximab) 
(HR, 0.70; 97.73% CI, 0.51–0.96; P = .01). One-year survival was also 
greater for patients who received nivolumab, relative to patients who 
received standard therapy (36.0% vs. 16.6%, respectively), and 
response rate was higher (13.3% vs. 5.8%, respectively), but median 
PFS was not significantly different between the two groups (2.0 vs. 2.3 
months, respectively; P = .32). In prespecified exploratory analyses, the

compared to the standard-of-care arm (8.4 vs. 6.9 months; HR, 0.80;

status, the results for OS were significantly better with pembrolizumab 
only for patients with tumors that have PD-L1 expression. A post hoc 
subgroup analysis of the KEYNOTE-040 trial evaluated outcomes in 
patients with recurrent-only (N = 125), recurrent and metastatic (N = 
204), or metastatic-only (N = 166) disease.734 Median OS for 
pembrolizumab compared to the standard-of-care arm in the recurrent-

5.1–9.6), respectively. In the recurrent and metastatic, and metastatic-

6.7 months (95% CI, 5.2–9.2) and 5.7 months (95% CI, 4.2–7.3), and 8.9

respectively. No differences in PFS were reported, regardless of 
treatment arm or subgroup. Exploratory health-related QOL analyses 
showed that patients treated with pembrolizumab had stable functioning 
and symptoms through 15 weeks, compared to the patients treated with 
standard of care, for whom a decline was observed.735 Pembrolizumab 
monotherapy was also evaluated for previously treated tumors with MSI-
high (MSI-H)/MMR deficiency (dMMR) in the phase II KEYNOTE-158 
basket trial, which included one patient with SCCHN.736 The ORR for the 
entire sample (N = 233) was 34.3% (95% CI, 28.3%–40.8%), median 
PFS was 4.1 months (95% CI, 2.4–4.9), and median OS was 23.5 
months (95% CI, 13.5 months–not reached). 

Pembrolizumab was initially studied at a dose of 10 mg/kg given every 2 
weeks in the SCCHN cohort of the KEYNOTE-012 trial, and clinical 
activity was identified.731 A lower, fixed-dose schedule using 
pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks was subsequently assessed in a 
phase 1b expansion cohort of 132 patients with recurrent or metastatic 
SCCHN.732 At 6 months, the OS rate was 59%, and the PFS was 23%, 
with an ORR of 18%. Observed responses appeared durable, although 
the follow-up was limited (median, 9 months). Pembrolizumab was also 
generally well-tolerated.731 Pooled analyses after long-term follow-up of 
the initial and expansion cohorts (N = 192) showed a 1-year OS rate of 
38%.733 Among the 34 patients with a disease response, 85% of the 
responses lasted ≥6 months, and 71% lasted ≥12 months. The FDA has 
approved an alternate dosing regimen of pembrolizumab 400 mg every 6 
weeks across all currently approved adult indications. 

The nonrandomized phase II KEYNOTE-055 trial studied pembrolizumab 
in 171 patients with SCCHN that progressed following treatment with 
both a platinum and cetuximab.737 The ORR was 16% (95% CI, 11%–
23%), and the mean duration of response was 8 months. 

Based on results of the phase Ib KEYNOTE-012 trial, pembrolizumab 
was evaluated in the phase III KEYNOTE-040 trial.697 Patients with 
recurrent or metastatic SCCHN (N = 495) were randomized to receive

randomized to receive afatinib had greater PFS compared to patients

vedotin-ejfv is an option following disease progression on or after platinum 
therapy and a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor. This is a category 2B 
recommendation based on the open-label phase II EV-202 trial, which 
evaluated the efficacy of enfortumab vedotin-ejfv in patients with 
recurrent/metastatic disease previously treated with platinum-based 
therapy and a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor.741 Study results showed an ORR of 
23.9%, DCR of 56.5%, and median DOR was not reached. Median PFS 
and OS were 3.9 and 6.0 months, respectively. Erdafitinib has also been 
included as an option for non-nasopharyngeal tumors with FGFR 
mutations or gene fusion-positive tumors and disease progression with at 
least one line of prior systemic therapy and no availability of an alternative 
systemic therapy. This is a category 2B recommendation and is based on 
the single-arm phase II RAGNAR study, which evaluated the efficacy and 
activity of erdafitinib in 217 previously treated patients with FGFR-mutated 
solid tumors.742 Only 15 of the 217 patients were diagnosed with SCCHN. 
Data showed a reduction in tumor burden for 159 (73%) participants. At a 
median follow-up for efficacy at 17.9 months, 30% (95% CI, 24–36) (n = 
64) of participants had an objective response, of which 6 (3%) had a 
complete response. For all other systemic therapy options recommended 
by the Panel, there are no clear advantages of one agent over another in 
the subsequent-line setting, although response rates seem to be highest 
with taxanes. Afatinib has a PFS benefit, but not an OS benefit, over 
methotrexate738 and is a category 2B systemic therapy option for non-
nasopharyngeal persistent H&N cancer or cancer that has progressed on 
or after platinum-containing chemotherapy. 

Occult Primary Cancer 

The Panel recommends immunotherapy (nivolumab and pembrolizumab) 
as the category 1 preferred option for patients with recurrent or metastatic 
SCCHN who have progressed on or following platinum-based 
chemotherapy, independent of CPS, based on high-quality evidence.697,698 
Pembrolizumab is also an option for treatment of MSI-H disease.736 Based 
on results from KEYNOTE-158,610 pembrolizumab is also FDA-approved 
for patients with previously treated TMB-H unresectable or metastatic 
disease that has progressed following prior treatment with no satisfactory 
treatment alternatives. Even though the basket trial contained no patients 
with TMB-H SCCHN, the Panel has included pembrolizumab for TMB-H 
disease as an option for patients with recurrent or metastatic SCCHN 
based on the FDA approval. Despite the ambiguities of PD-L1 testing and 
definitions, PD-L1 expression may be associated with better outcomes 
from treatment with immunotherapy for recurrent or metastatic SCCHN (ie, 
greater likelihood of response to pembrolizumab and greater survival 
benefit in response to nivolumab). The Panel included fam-trastuzumab 
deruxtecan-nxki for HER2-positive disease (in the subsequent-line setting 
with no satisfactory alternative treatment options) based on the 2024 FDA 
approval for all solid tumors. However, the DESTINY-PanTumor02 basket 
trial included <5 patients with non-salivary H&N cancers.740 Therefore, this 
is a category 2B option based on less Panel consensus. Enfortumab 

Occult or unknown primary H&N cancer is defined as metastatic 
carcinoma in a cervical lymph node without an identifiable primary site 
after appropriate investigation. This is an uncommon disease entity, 
accounting for approximately 5% of patients presenting to referral centers. 
The most frequent histology is SCC. Although patients with very small 

MS-60

pages.title: Head and Neck Cancers
pages.text:
tonsil and tongue base cancers frequently present with enlarged neck 
nodes and are initially classified as having an unknown primary, most will 
eventually be diagnosed by directed biopsy and tonsillectomy. The 
emergence of the primary site after therapy and during follow-up is rare. 
H&N cancer of unknown primary site is a highly curable disease. After 
appropriate evaluation and treatment, most patients experience low 
morbidity and long-term disease control. 

Workup 

When a needle biopsy shows SCC, adenocarcinoma, or 
anaplastic/undifferentiated epithelial cancer without a primary site, 
additional studies are needed (see Occult Primary in the algorithm). High-
risk HPV and EBV testing are recommended for squamous cell or 
undifferentiated histology, and p16+ unknown primary disease should only 
be considered HPV-positive with HPV-specific testing.601,745-749 High-risk 
HPV and EBV testing can be useful in workup and management of 
cancers of the neck of unknown primary, and patients with EBV- or HPV-
related cervical adenopathy are staged according to the classification for 
nasopharyngeal and HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer, 
respectively.750,751 

The majority of patients >40 years of age who present with a neck mass 
prove to have malignant lymph node involvement. In situations where 
metastatic carcinoma is found in cervical lymph nodes, the primary site is 
almost always discovered in the course of a complete H&N examination 
and imaging evaluation. FNA is the preferred diagnostic procedure when a 
malignant cervical lymph node is suspected. FNA obtained from cystic and 
necrotic lymph nodes may be non-diagnostic, and, in these situations, a 
core biopsy may be obtained. Open biopsy should not be performed 
unless the patient is prepared for definitive surgical management of the 
malignancy, which may entail a neck dissection, and patients should be 
counseled accordingly in the preoperative period. 

A thorough operative examination of at-risk mucosal sites is an important 
component in the workup of a patient with an occult primary, especially in 
scenarios where CT or PET imaging do not reveal the primary site. During 
this procedure, directed biopsies of areas of mucosal abnormalities 
suspicious for the primary site are undertaken. Randomly directed 
biopsies of normal-appearing mucosa in potential primary sites have a low 
yield and seldom disclose a primary cancer. Many primary cancers are 
identified after tonsillectomy. However, the therapeutic benefit of this 
surgery is uncertain because, when patients have been treated without 
tonsillectomy, only a few develop a clinically significant primary tumor. 

Treatment 

Patients with a biopsy-proven carcinoma of a cervical lymph node require 
a thorough history with emphasis on tobacco exposure; prior cancer 
history, including previously resected early-stage cutaneous malignancies; 
and ethnic descent from endemic NPC regions. A physical examination 
documenting cervical lymph node levels may inform potential primary 
sites. These patients require dedicated imaging of the H&N. This can be 
accomplished through contrast-enhanced CT imaging. An FDG-PET/CT 
may reveal a primary site not visible on contrast-enhanced CT 
imaging.743,744 

Neck dissection is recommended for all patients with 
thyroglobulin-negative and calcitonin-negative adenocarcinoma (see 
Occult Primary in the algorithm). If the metastatic adenocarcinoma 
presents high in the neck, parotidectomy may be included with the neck 
dissection. After neck dissection, management depends on the findings 
(ie, N1 without ENE, N2 or N3 without ENE, or ENE) (see Occult Primary 
in the algorithm). 

MS-61

pages.title: Head and Neck Cancers
pages.text:
Salivary Gland Tumors 

Salivary gland tumors can arise in the major salivary glands (ie, parotid, 
submandibular, sublingual) or in one of the minor salivary glands, which 
are widely spread throughout the aerodigestive tract.754 Many minor 
salivary gland tumors are located on the hard palate. Approximately 20% 
of the parotid gland tumors are malignant; the incidence of malignancy in 
submandibular and minor salivary gland tumors is approximately 50% and 
80%, respectively. These malignant tumors constitute a broad spectrum of 
histologic types, including mucoepidermoid, acinic, adenocarcinoma, 
adenoid cystic carcinoma, malignant myoepithelial tumors, and SCC. The 
primary diagnosis of SCC of the parotid gland is rare; however, the parotid 
gland is a frequent site of metastasis from skin cancer.755 Prognosis and 
tendency to metastasize vary among these histologic types. Major 
prognostic factors are histologic grade, tumor size, and local invasion. 
Staging is done using the 8th edition of the AJCC Cancer Staging 
Manual.43 

Due to the infrequency of this disease, high-level prospective evidence to 
guide clinical management is lacking. Among NCCN Member Institutions, 
significant variation exists regarding the management of SCC, poorly 
differentiated or nonkeratinizing SCC, anaplastic cancer (not thyroid) of 
unknown primary site, or other uncommon histologies. The Panel 
members believe such patients should be treated with a neck dissection. 
RT is also an option for patients with N1 disease, as a retrospective 
single-institution study showed that IMRT in patients with cervical lymph 
node metastasis from an unknown primary was associated with good local 
control and survival outcomes.752 Among N2–3 SCC with occult primary 
that are not managed surgically, recommendations are based on less 
Panel consensus: concurrent systemic therapy/RT (category 2B) or 
induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation or RT (category 3). A 
neck dissection may be recommended after treatment with RT and/or 
systemic therapy, depending on the clinical response. Since HPV-positive 
occult primary is likely located in the tonsil or base of tongue regions, 
radiation targets may be limited to these mucosal regions (see Cancer of 
the Oropharynx [p16 (HPV)-positive] in the algorithm).466 

Treatment 

Postoperative therapy among patients with occult primary SCC is based 
on the amount of nodal disease and the presence or absence of ENE. For 
N1 disease without ENE, NCCN Panel members recommend either: 1) RT 
that encompasses the target volume; or 2) careful observation with regular 
H&N examinations. Postoperative RT or consideration of concurrent 
chemoradiation (category 2B for chemoradiation) is recommended for N2 
or N3 disease without ENE (see Occult Primary in the algorithm). For 
ENE, concurrent chemoradiation is a category 1 recommendation; RT 
alone is an option (see Occult Primary in the algorithm).139,140 

The major therapeutic approach for salivary gland tumors is adequate and 
appropriate surgical resection.756-759 Surgical intervention requires careful 
planning and execution, particularly in parotid tumor surgery because the 
facial nerve is in the gland. The gland should be preserved if the nerve is 
not directly involved by the tumor. Most parotid gland tumors are located in 
the superficial lobe. If the facial nerve is functioning preoperatively, the 
nerve can be preserved in most patients.760 The facial nerve should be 
sacrificed if there is preoperative facial nerve involvement with facial palsy 
or if there is direct invasion of the tumor into the nerve where the tumor 
cannot be separated from the nerve. Malignant deep lobe parotid tumors 
are rare; however, they are generally a challenge for the surgeon because 
the patient may require superficial parotidectomy and identification and 
retraction of the facial nerve to remove the deep lobe parotid tumor. 

Definitive and postoperative treatment of EBV-positive disease should be 
treated as nasopharyngeal cancer (see Cancer of the Nasopharynx in the 
algorithm).753 

MS-62

pages.title: Head and Neck Cancers
pages.text:
Systemic Therapy 
Targeted systemic therapy is increasingly becoming an option for patients 
with distant metastatic salivary gland tumors. NGS and other biomarker 
tests should be used to evaluate at least the following: AR, NTRK1/2/3, 
FGFR, BRAF, RET, MSI, dMMR, TMB, PD-L1, and HER2 status.610,742,768-

779 Since HER2-testing guidelines are currently not available for patients 
with salivary gland cancers, the Panel refers to the ASCO/CAP guidelines 
for HER2-testing of breast cancers (https://www.cap.org/protocols-and-
guidelines/cap-guidelines/current-cap-guidelines/recommendations-for-
human-epidermal-growth-factor-2-testing-in-breast-cancer). 

For inoperable tumors, the Panel recommends highly conformal RT 
techniques such as IMRT, protons, or other heavy ions for definitive 
radiation treatment. Results from a retrospective cohort study including 
545 patients with salivary gland tumors treated between 1997 and 2010 
showed better local control and survival outcomes with neutron therapy, 
relative to photon therapy.761 However, risk of late effects with neutron 
therapy is high and tends to increase over time, with estimates as high as 
20% at 9 years.762,763 Neutron therapy is no longer routinely recommended 
for treatment of salivary gland cancers due to the diminishing demand, 
concerns regarding the methodologic robustness of available randomized 
trial data, and closure of all but one center in the United States. The Panel 
recognizes the potential clinical value of neutron therapy for select 
patients. 

A significant number of advanced salivary gland tumors with distant 
metastases are androgen receptor-positive (AR+).770-774 Therefore, the 
Panel recommends that patients with tumors that are AR+ receive 
androgen receptor therapy (ie, leuprolide, bicalutamide, abiraterone, 
goserelin).774,780-783 

Most malignant deep lobe parotid tumors will require postoperative RT 
because of adverse pathologic features such as the limitations of surgical 
margins in the resection of these tumors.756,758,764 RT is also used in an 
adjuvant setting for tumors with other adverse pathologic features (eg, 
intermediate, T3–4 tumors, or positive lymph nodes)757,765,766; systemic 
therapy/RT (category 2B) can also be considered.767 Efficacy data for 
systemic therapy/RT for patients with advanced salivary gland tumors that 
have been resected are limited. Extensive safety data are available and 
may be extrapolated from the management of SCCHN, with some NCCN 
Member Institutions using platinum-based regimens for these patients. 
With regard to unresectable salivary gland tumors, the NCCN Panel had 
less consensus about chemoradiation (which is reflected in the category 
2B recommendations), because there are few published trials. Clinical 
trials are ongoing in this area (eg, Clinical trial IDs: NCT01220583, 
NCT02776163). 

Two phase I/II studies including patients with advanced NTRK gene 
fusion-positive cancer (with 22%–38% being salivary gland tumors, 
particularly secretory carcinoma) showed promising ORRs of 75% to 
100% with the TRK inhibitor larotrectinib.775,776 A pooled analysis from a 
phase II trial and two phase I trials including 54 patients with NTRK gene 
fusion-positive cancer (13% being mammary analogue secretory 
carcinoma of the salivary gland) showed an ORR of 57.4% for entrectinib, 
another TRK inhibitor.777 Finally, repotrectinib was evaluated in a phase I/II 
study including 88 patients with NTRK gene fusion-positive advanced solid 
tumors (48 previously treated with a TRK TKI, and 40 who were TRK TKI-
naïve).784 Eleven patients (12.5%) had a salivary gland tumor. The 
analysis showed an ORR of 58% for those who were TRK TKI-naïve, and 
50% in those who were previously treated with a TRK TKI. The FDA 
approved larotrectinib, entrectinib, and repotrectinib for treatment of 
patients with NTRK gene fusion-positive tumors, and the Panel also 

MS-63

pages.title: Head and Neck Cancers
pages.text:
recommends these three NTRK1/2/3 therapy options for patients with 
recurrent NTRK gene fusion-positive salivary gland tumors and distant 
metastases. 

phase I study that included 8 participants with salivary gland tumors793; the 
Japanese MYTHOS trial, including 9 participants with salivary gland 
tumors794; and a case series including 8 patients with HER2-low or HER2-
mutant salivary gland tumors.795 

Pembrolizumab is an option for patients with previously treated TMB-H, 
MSI-H/dMMR recurrent, unresectable, or metastatic salivary gland cancer, 
based on results from the phase II KEYNOTE-158 trial, which included 
three patients with salivary gland cancer and TMB-H (≥10 mut/Mb) 
disease610 and two patients with MSI-H/dMMR advanced salivary gland 
cancer.736 Combination dabrafenib/trametinib is FDA-approved for all 
advanced BRAF V600E-mutated tumors, and a case report supports its 
use for widely metastatic salivary duct carcinoma that is BRAF V600E-
mutated.778 Similarly, selpercatinib is FDA-approved for all locally 
advanced or metastatic RET gene fusion-positive solid tumors, and its use 
for patients with recurrent, unresectable, or metastatic salivary gland 
cancer is supported by the ongoing phase I/II LIBRETTO-001 trial, which, 
at the time of the most recent analysis, included 4 patients with a salivary 
gland tumor and an ORR of 50% for these patients (independent review 
committee assessment).779 Erdafitinib has also been included as an option 
for recurrent, unresectable, or metastatic salivary gland tumors with FGFR 
mutations or gene-fusion positive tumors (category 2B).742 A 100% ORR 
and DCR were reported for the five individuals with salivary gland tumors 
included in the phase IIb RAGNAR study. 

Other systemic therapy options may be used for palliation in advanced 
disease. Various combinations of chemotherapy agents (ie, 
cisplatin/cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin, cisplatin/vinorelbine, 
carboplatin/paclitaxel, carboplatin/gemcitabine) have been shown in small 
series to be active for some salivary gland malignant histologies, with 
ORRs ranging from 24% to 60%.796-800 A small phase II trial also supports 
use of paclitaxel monotherapy based on an ORR of 26% for patients with 

HER2 positivity has also been found in some advanced salivary gland 
tumors.772,774,785 It is recommended that these patients receive a HER2-
targeted treatment option such as trastuzumab and trastuzumab-based 
combinations.774,786 Small series demonstrate that ado-trastuzumab 
emtansine is active in patients with previously treated metastatic HER2-
positive salivary gland cancers.787,788 Nonrandomized phase II trials have 
also examined trastuzumab combined with other agents for patients with 
advanced HER2-positive salivary gland cancers. For example, results 
from an open-label, single-center, phase II Japanese study including 57 
patients with recurrent or metastatic HER2-positive salivary gland cancer 
showed that trastuzumab combined with docetaxel was associated with a 
70.2% ORR (95% CI, 56.6%–81.6%).789 Complete response was reached 
in 14% of patients, partial response was reached in 56.1%, and stable 
disease was observed in 24.6%. The median PFS was 8.9 months (95% 
CI, 7.8–9.9), and OS was 39.7 months (95% CI, not reached). A significant 
number of grade 3 or 4 adverse events were reported in this study (89%, 
with grade 4 adverse events being reported in 61%). The most common 
serious adverse events were hematologic: decreased white blood cell, 
neutrophil, and lymphocyte counts. Results from the ongoing open-label 
phase II MyPathway basket study, including 16 patients with advanced 
HER2-positive, -overexpressed, or -amplified salivary gland cancers, 
showed that pertuzumab combined with trastuzumab was associated with 
a 60% ORR.790 Median duration of response for these patients was 9.2 
months, and the regimen was well-tolerated (ie, only one grade 3 TRAE). 
In a pooled analysis of two studies including 17 patients with HER2-
positive salivary duct carcinoma, fam-trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki was 
associated with an ORR of 47% (all partial responses).791,792 Fam-
trastuzumab deruxtecan-nxki is also supported by a dose-expansion, 

MS-64

pages.title: Head and Neck Cancers
pages.text:
factors specific to MM: 1) the poor prognosis of MM even with a limited 
burden of disease from the primary tumor; and 2) there is still some 
gradation of survival based on the burden of disease as reflected in local, 
regional, and distant extent. Thus, the AJCC staging system for MM 
begins with T3, N0 disease as the most limited form of disease (T staging 
similar to anaplastic thyroid carcinoma), and the staging reflects the 
biological aggressiveness of the tumor, local burden of disease, as well as 
regional and distant extent. In addition, the AJCC staging system reflects 
the fact that MM occurs at all mucosal sites in the H&N. Therefore, rules 
for classifying, staging, and surgical principles should be based on the 
appropriate anatomical site of origin. Workup for these tumors is described 
in the NCCN Guidelines for Head and Neck Cancers. Molecular profiling of 
MM is highly recommended to facilitate consideration of neoadjuvant or 
adjuvant systemic therapies. 

mucoepidermoid or adenocarcinoma histology; no responses were 
observed for adenoid cystic carcinoma.801 Use of certain tyrosine kinase 
inhibitors such as axitinib (with or without avelumab) and sorafenib have 
been evaluated in nonrandomized phase II trials802-804 and are 
recommended by the Panel as category 2B options for patients with 
unresectable, metastatic, or recurrent salivary gland tumors (useful in 
certain circumstances). Sunitinib805 and dovitinib806 have also been 
evaluated in phase II trials, but larger trials are needed to determine the 
efficacy of these options. Lenvatinib as a treatment option for recurrent or 
metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma has been evaluated in two phase II 
trials, which showed DCRs of 88% (partial response of 11.5%–15.6%, 
stable disease in 75%–76.9%).807,808 Based on these results and lack of 
other evidence-based options for recurrent or metastatic adenoid cystic 
carcinoma, lenvatinib is a category 2B option. 

Treatment 

Mucosal Melanoma of the Head and Neck 

MM is a rare but highly aggressive neoplasm with a poor prognosis.809,810 It 
occurs throughout the upper aerodigestive tract.811 Most MM (70%–80%) 
occur in the nasal cavity or paranasal sinuses, followed by the oral cavity, 
pharynx, and larynx.812 The incidence of nasal cavity MM appears to be 
increasing.809 Sinonasal MM is typically confined to the primary site at 
presentation.813 Oral cavity MM more frequently presents with clinically 
apparent lymph node metastasis.814 No etiologic risk factors are yet 
apparent. Recent genomic studies have identified distinct molecular 
characteristics of MM, including frequent mutations in NRAS (15%–19%), 
KIT (7%–26%), and NF1 (18%), with lower rates of BRAF mutations (5%–
8%) compared to cutaneous melanoma.815-817 Recurrent structural 
variations and amplifications in CDK4, MDM2, and TERT are common. 

Workup and Staging 

Although limited data exist on treatment options, primary treatment should 
be surgical for T3, N0–1 and T4a, N0–1 disease. For T4b disease, 
although surgery is not generally considered, a multidisciplinary team 
discussion is suggested to ensure appropriate care.818 Neck dissection 
with postoperative radiation is recommended for clinical nodal 
disease.819,820 Postoperative radiation to the primary site is typically 
indicated in most cases, as there is evidence that it improves local control. 
Postoperative RT to the neck depends on the extent of nodal 
involvement.821-823 A large combined analysis of 300 patients with 
sinonasal MM demonstrated that postoperative RT significantly improved 
relapse-free survival (15.2 vs. 9.8 months; HR, 0.714; P = .014), 
particularly in patients with T4a or stage IVA disease.824 NCCN strongly 
encourages clinical trials for all patients with MM to better define treatment 
choices at all stages of the disease. 

The 8th edition of the AJCC Cancer Staging Manual includes a staging 
system for MM (see Table 9).43 The AJCC staging recognizes two key 

MS-65

pages.title: Head and Neck Cancers
pages.text:
Radiation Therapy 
The role of RT in MM has not been evaluated in prospective trials. 
However, results of a randomized trial in cutaneous melanoma are 
considered relevant to MM in the postoperative setting after surgery at the 
primary site or neck dissection (see third paragraph in this section).825 
Local recurrence is common after surgery alone in MM. After using 
postoperative radiation, lower rates of local and neck recurrence have 
been reported in historical comparison series.823,826-829 In unresectable or 
medically inoperable cases, reasonable local control outcomes using RT 
followed by systemic therapy have been reported in small cohort series of 
MMs.830-832 

Considering this trial and retrospective studies in MM, the NCCN Panel 
recommends postoperative RT for the following high-risk features: ENE, 
involvement of two or more neck or intraparotid nodes, any node ≥3 cm, or 
recurrence in the neck or soft tissue after initial surgical resection.833,834 
Conventional fractionation is recommended (at 2 Gy per fraction to a total 
postoperative dose of 60–66 Gy). The Australian-New Zealand 
randomized trial used 48 Gy in 20 fractions (240 cGy/fraction) to the neck, 
axilla, or groin.825 However, the NCCN Panel prefers conventional 
fractionation to somewhat higher total doses (60–66 Gy) in the neck 
because of concerns about late effects from larger dose per fraction, 
which may not be fully expressed for many years after treatment. The 
following schedules may also be used: 1) 48–50 Gy (2.4–3 Gy/fraction); or 
2) 30–36 Gy (6 Gy/fraction).825,826,834 

Primary size or thickness is not used as a risk factor when considering RT 
to the primary site; all invasive primaries are considered at high risk for 
local recurrence. For sinonasal primary sites, target volumes may include 
the primary site without elective treatment of the neck (see Mucosal 
Melanoma in the algorithm). Because oral cavity primary sites are felt to 
be at a higher risk for disease progression in the neck, elective 
management with neck dissection and/or RT may be applied, although this 
is not routinely done (see Mucosal Melanoma in the algorithm). 

RT is often recommended in the postoperative management of MMs. 
Indications for postoperative radiation to the neck are generally 
extrapolated from cutaneous melanoma. An Australian-New Zealand 
consortium reported on a randomized trial (250 patients) of postoperative 
RT versus observation in patients with palpable adenopathy from 
cutaneous primaries. Postoperative RT was associated with a significant 
reduction in relapse in the nodal basin (19% vs. 31%) and a significant 
improvement in lymph node field control.825 Disease relapsed in only 20 
patients who received RT, whereas disease relapsed in 34 patients who 
were under observation only (P = .04). However, no significant differences 
in OS were reported. 

IMRT may be very useful in helping to achieve homogenous dose 
distributions and to spare critical organs, especially in paranasal sinus 
sites.235,678,835 3D-CRT may also be used, but IMRT is preferred. Reports 
suggest that the use of hypofractionation in cutaneous melanomas (which 
is convenient) is associated with good outcomes but no clear advantage in 
cancer control. Little experience is available using large dose per fraction 
in mucosal sites. Because of the close proximity of neural structures and 
risk of late effects, hypofractionation (if used) must be carefully planned 
and delivered.835 RT should not be used concurrently with BRAF/MEK 
inhibitor therapy, as concurrent use has been found to be associated with 
grade ≥3 dermatologic reactions, and potentially lethal hemorrhaging in 
the liver, lung, and brain have all been reported.836 For primary sites in the 
paranasal sinuses and nasal cavity, PBT should be considered due to the 
proximity of eye and other vital structures. A recent study of 
hypofractionated spot-scanning proton therapy (60–64 Gy [relative 
biological effectiveness (RBE)] in 15–16 fractions) for sinonasal MM has 
demonstrated 3-year local control rates of 83% with acceptable toxicity, 
though distant metastasis remains the primary pattern of failure.837 

MS-66

pages.title: Head and Neck Cancers
pages.text:
demonstrated an ORR of 45% and median PFS of 8.2 months in a phase 
II study of 43 patients with advanced MM.841 The benefit of this 
combination is likely due to the vascularized nature of MM and the 
immunosuppressive effects of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). 

Systemic Therapy 
Systemic therapy used for cutaneous melanoma (eg, immunotherapy) is 
recommended for MM (see Systemic Therapy for Metastatic or 
Unresectable Disease in the NCCN Guidelines for Melanoma: Cutaneous, 
available at www.NCCN.org). 

Follow-up 

Recommendations for surveillance are provided in the algorithm (see 
Follow-up Recommendations in the algorithm). Note that physical 
examination for MM should include endoscopic inspection for nasal cavity 
and paranasal sinus disease. 

There is currently no standard approach for systemic therapy treatment of 
resectable MM. Adjuvant systemic immunotherapy is an option for MM 
with nodal involvement. While the majority of patients in melanoma 
adjuvant trials had cutaneous primaries, some patients with MM were 
included. Adjuvant chemotherapy may also be considered. A phase III 
randomized trial of 204 patients with resected MM demonstrated that 
adjuvant temozolomide plus cisplatin significantly improved relapse-free 
survival (15.5 vs. 9.9 months; HR, 0.622; P = .001) and distant metastasis-
free survival (19.5 vs. 12.7 months; HR, 0.705; P = .025) compared to 
high-dose interferon alpha-2b.838 

Neoadjuvant checkpoint inhibitor for MM is not well-studied. Recent data 
suggest, however, that neoadjuvant therapy for resectable MM is a 
feasible approach with signs of efficacy and an acceptable safety profile. 
Further investigation is needed.839 More recently, data demonstrate 
improvements in EFS with neoadjuvant and adjuvant pembrolizumab over 
adjuvant pembrolizumab alone in patients with resectable stage III/IV 
melanoma.840 While this study included only a small number of patients 
with MM, it is not known whether this approach is of value for this 
particular melanoma subtype, though it may be useful in certain situations 
(ie, large symptomatic disease burden). 

For advanced or metastatic MM, immunotherapy with anti-PD-1 agents 
remains first-line therapy, though response rates are lower than in 
cutaneous melanoma (see the NCCN Guidelines for Melanoma: 
Cutaneous; available at www.NCCN.org). Combination strategies may 
also be promising. In particular, atezolizumab plus bevacizumab

nodes.text: The comprehensive care of patients with head and neck cancers is complex. All patients need access to the full range of support services and specialists with expertise in the comprehensive care of patients with head and neck cancer for optimal treatment and follow-up. Outcomes are improved when patients with head and neck cancers are treated at high-volume centers.
lines: The comprehensive care of patients with head and neck cancers is complex. All patients need access to the full range of support services and
specialists with expertise in the comprehensive care of patients with head and neck cancer for optimal treatment and follow-up. Outcomes are

footnotes.text: Principles of Surgery (SURG-A).
Tumors in the base of tongue, posterior pharyngeal wall, and soft palate require consideration of bilateral neck treatment as do tumors of the tonsil invading the tongue base.

For pN0–N1 and no poor pathologic risk features, single-modality treatment should be considered whenever possible. For T1–T2 primary tumors near midline and resected to adequate margins and with no adverse pathologic features, a staged contralateral neck dissection can be performed in order to avoid RT. Lateral tumors pN0–N1 resected with favorable pathologic features can be observed.

For nonkeratinizing or undifferentiated histology, consider testing for EBV in tumor tissue and blood. Common means for detecting EBV in pathologic specimens include ISH for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) or IHC staining for latent membrane protein (LMP). The EBV DNA load within the serum or plasma may be quantified using PCR targeting genomic sequences of the EBV DNA such as BamHI-W, Epstein-Barr virus nuclear antigen (EBNA), or LMP; these tests vary in their sensitivity. The EBV DNA load may reflect prognosis and change in response to therapy.

primary_site.definition: Anatomic site of the primary tumor as stated in the case.

histology.definition: Histologic diagnosis of the primary or of a neck node (biopsy or FNA).

clinical_t_category.definition: Clinical T category of the primary tumor.

clinical_n_category.definition: Clinical N category of regional nodes. N2c is bilateral disease.

m_category.definition: Distant metastasis status at presentation or at recurrence work-up.

m_category_at_diagnosis.definition: Distant metastasis status at the time of initial diagnosis (initial presentation).

metastatic_pattern.definition: Extent of distant metastatic disease, as judged by the clinician from the case.

disease_setting.definition: Whether the cancer is newly diagnosed, a locoregional recurrence, persistent disease after treatment, or a second primary.

prior_head_and_neck_radiotherapy.definition: True if the patient has received prior radiotherapy to the head and neck region.

locoregional_disease_present.definition: True if locoregional (primary or regional nodal) recurrent or persistent disease is present.

ecog_score.definition: ECOG performance status (0 to 4) as recorded in the case.

hpv_p16_status.definition: Tumor HPV status by p16 IHC (p16 positive is HPV-positive surrogate).

ebv_status.definition: Epstein-Barr virus status of the tumor (EBV or EBER positive/negative).

primary_tumor_identified.definition: True if the primary tumor has been found on exam, biopsy, or imaging; false for a neck node with unknown primary.

clinically_benign.definition: True if the lesion is judged clinically benign on work-up.

most_inferior_involved_neck_level.definition: The most inferior neck level containing clinically involved nodes (levels ordered I to V_lower).

clinical_ipsilateral_involved_node_count.definition: Number of clinically involved ipsilateral lymph nodes on imaging or exam.

largest_clinical_involved_node_diameter_.definition: Diameter in cm of the largest clinically involved lymph node.

thyroglobulin_negative.definition: True if thyroglobulin is negative on work-up of a neck adenocarcinoma.

calcitonin_negative.definition: True if calcitonin is negative on work-up of a neck adenocarcinoma.

neoadjuvant_pembrolizumab_received.definition: True if the patient has received neoadjuvant pembrolizumab before surgery.

definitive_treatment_received.definition: Definitive (primary-intent) treatment the patient has already received for this cancer.

treatment_completed.definition: True if the planned treatment for this cancer has been completed (follow-up phase).

neck_dissection_performed.definition: True if a neck dissection has been performed for this cancer.

pd_l1_cps.definition: PD-L1 combined positive score (CPS) of the tumor.

induction_chemo_response.definition: Response of the primary site to induction chemotherapy.

neck_response_after_induction.definition: Response of the neck disease after induction chemotherapy.

response_to_prior_treatment.definition: Overall response of the disease to previously received treatment.

resectable.definition: Clinician judgement: the primary and nodal disease can be resected and resection is recommended. False for unresectable primary or nodal disease.

nodal_disease_resectable.definition: Clinician judgement: the regional nodal disease can be resected. False for unresectable nodal disease.

amenable_to_larynx_preserving_surgery.definition: Clinician judgement: the laryngeal tumor is amenable to larynx-preserving (conservation) surgery.

requires_total_laryngectomy.definition: Clinician judgement: the laryngeal tumor requires (is amenable to) total laryngectomy.

requires_pharyngectomy.criteria: Requiring (amenable to) pharyngectomy with partial or total laryngectomy
requires_pharyngectomy.definition: Clinician judgement: the hypopharyngeal tumor requires (is amenable to) pharyngectomy with partial or total laryngectomy.

requires_pharyngectomy_with_total_laryng.criteria: Advanced cancer requiring (amenable to) pharyngectomy with total laryngectomy
requires_pharyngectomy_with_total_laryng.definition: Clinician judgement: the hypopharyngeal tumor requires (is amenable to) pharyngectomy with total laryngectomy.

unfit_for_surgery.definition: Clinician judgement: the patient is unfit for surgery.

declines_surgery.definition: True if the patient declines surgery.

medically_unfit_for_systemic_therapy.criteria: not a medical candidate for concurrent systemic therapy/RT
medically_unfit_for_systemic_therapy.definition: Clinician judgement: the patient is not a medical candidate for systemic therapy (or systemic therapy/RT).

further_resection_possible.definition: Clinician judgement: further resection of residual disease is feasible.

resection_completeness.definition: Completeness of the resection of the tumor. Incomplete without residual disease means no residual disease on exam, imaging, and/or endoscopy.

margin_status.definition: Pathologic status of the surgical margin.

extranodal_extension.definition: True if pathology shows extranodal extension of nodal metastasis.

lymphovascular_invasion.definition: True if pathology shows lymphatic or vascular invasion.

perineural_invasion.definition: True if pathology shows neural or perineural invasion.

pathologic_t_category.definition: Pathologic T category of the primary tumor after resection.

pathologic_n_category.definition: Pathologic N category after neck dissection.

positive_lymph_node_count.definition: Number of pathologically positive lymph nodes in the neck dissection specimen.

pathologic_nodal_level_iv_or_v_involved.definition: True if pathology shows nodal disease in neck levels IV or V.

tumor_adjacent_cribriform_plate_or_media.definition: True if the tumor is adjacent to the cribriform plate and/or the medial wall of the orbit.

sentinel_lymph_node_result.definition: Result of sentinel lymph node biopsy.

values: Cancer of the Oral Cavity (Including Mucosal Lip)
Very Advanced Head and Neck Cancer
guideline_section.definition: Which disease or subtype section of this guideline the case belongs to: the disease named in the guideline's page headings that the patient has (e.g. the tumor type or subtype).

adverse_pathologic_features.definition: True if any of the printed adverse pathologic features is present: extranodal extension, close or positive margin, lymphatic/vascular invasion, neural/perineural invasion, or intermediate or high grade. Site-specific items printed only for salivary tumors are handled in predicates on raw facts.

nodal_volume_category.definition: Clinical nodal disease volume on the ipsilateral side: one node of 3 cm or less; one node over 3 cm, or two or more ipsilateral nodes of 6 cm or less; otherwise other.

low_volume_disease.definition: Low-volume disease as printed in the flowchart: clinical T1 or T2 with clinical N1.

clinical_node_positive.definition: Clinically node-positive disease (any clinical N category other than N0).

pathologic_node_positive.definition: Pathologically node-positive disease: at least one positive node, or pN1 or higher.

pd_l1_cps_positive.definition: PD-L1 positive, defined as CPS of 1 or more as printed in the boxes.

other_risk_features_from_findings.definition: Other risk features as printed in the footnotes: margins, pT3 or pT4 primary, pN2 or pN3 nodal disease, nodal disease in levels IV or V, perineural invasion, vascular invasion, and lymphatic invasion.

salivary_adverse_pathologic_features_fro.definition: Salivary gland adverse pathologic features as printed in the box: intermediate or high grade; close or positive margins; neural/perineural invasion; lymph node metastases; lymphatic/vascular invasion; high-grade T3-4a tumors.

ethmoid_adverse_pathologic_features_from.definition: Ethmoid sinus adverse pathologic features as printed in the box: positive margins, close margins (tumors adjacent to the cribriform plate and/or medial wall of the orbit), and unfavorable histology (intermediate or high grade; favorable histology includes low grade).

notes.predicates: Conditions were drafted and reviewed by a language model (model_reviewed), not by clinicians. 'rejected' means the review rejected the draft; the box then needs clinician judgement. 'section_only' means the box only requires the patient to be in the page's guideline section.
notes.coordinates: bbox and line_bboxes are PDF points with the origin at the page's top left; pages[].size gives the page size.
notes.links: page links name a page id from pages[]; a multi-page code such as PROS-F has ids 'PROS-F 1 of 5' ... ; external_guideline links name another guideline's slug.
